Rev1 - App DI ROW 255 | 9: The Modus software shall support 7 operating modes:
·        Initialisation 
·        Warm up
·        Monitoring
·        Configuration
·        Data Analysis
·        Emergency Alarms
·        Error state (Measurement Mode and power up/down states)
Rev1 - App DI ROW 256 | 9: The Monitoring Mode is the primary mode of the application, where it continuously collects and displays glucose readings from the CGM device. This mode includes the following features:
·        Real-time glucose monitoring: The application fetches and displays real-time glucose readings from the CGM device, providing users with up-to-date information.
·        Glucose trend analysis: The application analyses the collected glucose data to provide trends and patterns, helping users understand their glucose levels over time.
·        Alerts and notifications: The application provides configurable user thresholds for low and high glucose levels to trigger notifications when glucose levels go above or below user set thresholds. 
·        The application provides non configurable low alarm, this is classified as critical alarm - See section [6.4.1.9] for further detail. 
·        Data syncing: The Application syncs data after encrypting it for secure transmission to server when received from transmitter.
·        Data storage and history: The application securely stores the collected glucose data for historical analysis and tracking. Users can access their past readings and trends through the application's interface. 
·        Error State: Handles the error states in the app, returning an error message to the user and going to the power down state if the error is fatal.
Rev1 - App DI ROW 257 | 9: The Configuration Mode allows users to customise settings and preferences within the application. This mode includes the following capabilities:
·        User profile management:
·        Alert configuration: Users can set their desired glucose threshold levels for high and low alerts and customise the associated alert types (e.g. sound, vibration). 
Rev1 - App DI ROW 258 | 9: The Data Analysis Mode enables users to perform in-depth analysis and generate reports based on their glucose data. This mode shall include the following functionalities:
·        Historical data visualisation: The application provides visual representations, such as charts or graphs, to help users analyse their glucose trends and patterns over specific time intervals.
·        Report generation: The application shall allow users to generate comprehensive reports summarising their glucose trends, patterns, and statistics for a given period.

Think detailed design. Permissions UI. Bluetooth and Location toggle UI. State based design and list the sensor states with relevant errors. | 8: Error handling mechanisms are in place to handle unexpected errors and exceptions, ensuring that the application does not crash and provides appropriate error messages or fallback options to the user.

Both applications calculate the percentage of measurements falling within each category over the selected time period, display the percentages to the user, and convert measurement counts to time durations (hours and minutes format) to show how long the user spent in each glucose range. | 8: The application analyses the collected glucose data to identify trends, patterns and fluctuations in glucose levels, allowing users to understand their glucose management better.
Unused DO ROW 188 | 1: DI-291 | 2: APP-SRS-6.1.5 | 3: Historical Glucose | 4: UN-17 Glucose Statistics | 5: The application must display an ambulatory glucose profile (AGP) chart | 6: Ambulatory glucose profile chart implementation
The iOS application implements AGP chart visualisation through AGPHorizotalViewController and AgpTVC view controllers, displaying glucose percentile ribbons calculated from historical measurement data.

The Android application displays an "Overall Glucose Profile (AGP-style)" percentile ribbon chart through the OverallGlucoseProfileChart composable component in the OGP Report screen. Both implementations aggregate glucose measurements over the selected time window to calculate and display the median, 25th/75th percentiles, and 10th/90th percentile ranges across a 24-hour period to show typical glucose patterns.
Unused DO ROW 189 | 1: DI-291 | 2: APP-SRS-6.1.5 | 3: Historical Glucose | 4: UN-17 Glucose Statistics | 5: The application must display a chart with the hourly average glucose measurement, for each hour in the 24 hour period. This must ensure that measurements considered for each displayed hour are centered and inclusive of measurements 30 minutes before and after (e.g. 1pm +- 30 minutes), so that the user can reasonably respond to their average when their clock shows the same time as on the chart. This must ensure that any timezone change is considered so that a consistent mealtime would remain consistently in the same bucket, regardless of timezone change. This must consider the impact of missing recent data points, and avoid displaying any entry if the average would not be updated and still relevant to the user. | 6: Hourly average glucose chart with timezone-aware display
The Android application calculates hourly averages by grouping glucose measurements into 24 hourly buckets (0-23) based on the device's system timezone. Each measurement's UTC timestamp is converted to the local hour using ZoneId.systemDefault(), ensuring that when the user views the chart at a specific time, the corresponding hourly average bucket reflects measurements that occurred during that local hour regardless of timezone. The application filters measurements by the selected data window (1, 15, or 30 days) using getMeasurementsWithDaysFilter, ensuring only recent relevant data contributes to the displayed averages.

The iOS application displays hourly data through view controllers that handle 24-hour period visualisation.

Both implementations use the device's current timezone for all timestamp conversions, which means if the user changes timezone, all historical measurements are re-interpreted in the new timezone, and consistent mealtimes remain in the same hourly bucket across timezone changes.

DI-DO ROW 4 | 3: UN-96 Trusted Distribution | 5: 267 | 6: 267 | 7: 649 | 8: The application must implement an internal update check mechanism and notify the user when the application has become outdated, in case the user has disabled automatic updates in the app stores or the update delivery is excessively delayed. | 9: Application Update Delivery | 10: Primary version availability, update notifications, and update rollout are handled by the App Store and Play Store respectively. This primary update channel includes functionality for staged roll out. 

When considering the app store and play store behaviours, there are a number of users who disable automatic updates (configured for each application), whether purposefully or accidentally  or forgotten. In this case the users will not receive automatic updates to the application through the standard platform mechanism. The procedure for a user to once again receive application updates in this scenario (including critical updates), is supported by a separate GlucoRx first-party internal version check API.

Note that automatic updates may be enabled but updates still not automatically installed due to application persistence features placing the application in an alive state where the system or updater is unwilling to update it (e.g. foreground service on Android), and in these cases the GlucoRx first-party internal version check API is also utilised to notify the user.

Due to the design of App Store and Play Store distribution, and the desire to use their staged rollout features, it is not immediately possible for the application to know when any new version update is available, even if the latest version was retained or fetched in the GlucoRx backend, noting that app store "latest release" APIs do not report staged rollout percentages. To address this deficiency, there are 4 levels of update checks depending on recall and update severity:
1) Optional updates not marked as "encouraged" or "recalled" through the recall API - Primary update channel remains responsible, with best-effort checks where the platform supports it periodically and before session start (before guidance to apply sensor) - This is currently Android only, through the "Google App Update Library", and is limited to phones with installed and updated Google Play services and with active internet connectivity. If a staged rollout is utilised this library will report the update to the user once it becomes available. If there is an update available on Android that the user has not installed automatically, it will be surfaced through the in-app UI and a low priority notification. iOS does not have such available functionality to check if an update is available to a given phone (staged rollout or not).
2) Updates marked as "encouraged" through the recall API. Where app fixes or improvements are substantial, the backend is configured to report these versions so both the iOS and Android applications can detect the available update (even if not-yet rolled out through staged release), and displays in-app UI directing the user to the relevant page of the app store where the update can be installed. This will be shown regardless of whether the user has automatic updates enabled, and will also help a user who has unintentionally disabled it to reconfigure that update setting. It is expected that updates are only marked as encouraged after staged roll outs are complete, and after time for the update to automatically install where possible, otherwise users will be told of an update that is not yet available to them.
3) Updates marked as "recalled - forbid next session" through the recall API. If the application version receives such a recall notice the current session is allowed to complete, after which new sessions cannot be started without performing an update (checked before sensor installation guidance tells the user to apply the sensor, in case it should not be applied before app update). The user is told through in-app UI after the check before sensor installation guidance (without any notification, not necessary as a session is not running). Note that a recall can be configured before an update is available, and in such cases the behaviour is the same, the user is told they need to update the application to continue and directed to the relevant platform app store regardless of update availability. Session resume is still permitted.
4) Updates marked as "recalled - stop immediately" through the recall API. If the application version receives such a recall notice the current session is not allowed to continue, measurements are no longer persisted or utilised by the application, and UI displays to inform the user they must update their application immediately, and the application immediately disconnects from any running CGM sensor session due to a recall of the application. No application features can be used other than the no-data alarm: the application process remains alive so the "no-data" alarm continues to function in this case to notify the user. Note that a recall can be configured before an update is available, and in such cases the behaviour is the same, the user is told they need to update the application to continue and directed to the relevant platform app store regardless of update availability.

Recall API calls are performed initially on each application start and also updated any time a "recall API change event" is received from the backend, and Google Play In-App Update API calls are performed periodically, as well as before starting a new session. Internet connectivity is required for the recall API but not for the Google Play In-App Update API. Caching behaviour and maximum age gates (when starting as session) for the recall API is defined in another DO, and Google Play Services is responsible for any caching of the latest available app update. If the Google Play In-App Update API call fails due to network errors then it is ignored (this is only ever used for optional updates not marked as "encouraged" or "recalled"). If the Google Play In-App update API check has failed due to an issue with Google Play services, the user is prompted to resolve these periodically through functionality provided by the library.
DI-DO ROW 5 | 1: DI-266 | 2: APP-SRS-5.1.3 | 3: UN-102 Device Support | 4: DI-3 | 5: 266 | 6: 266 | 7: 650 | 8: All core features must support consecutive mobile operating system versions covering a market share total of at least 90%. | 9: OS Market Share Evaluation | 10: For the initial application release, the supported OS version range is evaluated against publicly available platform distribution data (App Store analytics for iOS and the Android distribution dashboard for Android) for the target geographic regions. The evaluation confirms that consecutive supported OS versions covers 90% of the target device population in those markets, noting that the publicly available statistics are an approximation.

When there is a new major version Android or iOS release GlucoRx considers when it is appropriate to stop distribution for the oldest versions, in such a way that maintains the device coverage target, considering maintenance costs and unavailable API features of older OS versions. This is done with the understanding that users with the application already installed will continue to have that version installed, however updates any new installs will no longer be available to them through the primary distribution channel. The internal version recall API is used to apply a killswitch when the build becomes too outdated.

The results of version evaluation, including data source, date, OS versions assessed, coverage percentage, and any proposed changes to the minimum deployment target are recorded in the release record.

There are many differences between different OS software across different manufacturers and model ranges and versions, and we have considered the following and minimised differences as far as possible; Google Play Services availability (fallbacks always implemented), Notification behaviour and styling (per manufacturer OS customisation), permission behaviour differences, keep alive differences (task kill behaviour and auto start preconditions), window decor theming differences, Bluetooth stack differences.

DI-DO ROW 9 | 1: DI-278 | 2: APP-SRS-5.2.3 | 3: UN-102 Device Support | 4: DI-7 | 5: 278 | 6: 278 | 7: 654 | 8: The iOS and Android app frameworks must be chosen to maximise the likelihood of performant, high quality applications, which are easy to maintain and support throughout the lifetime of the product. | 9: Native Platform Framework | 10: The application is implemented using the native platform framework and language for each target platform. No cross-platform runtime (React Native, Flutter, Xamarin) is used for any feature layer to ensure the application performance is very high, and without undue bugs, and platform differences are easier to support and maintain with dedicated platform developers.

iOS framework stack uses Swift with SwiftUI as the primary view layer, CoreBluetooth for BLE communication, Core Data for on-phone data persistence and source of truth.

Android framework stack relies on many widely used officially supported dependencies; Kotlin with Jetpack Compose to allow a reliable state-based architecture, native Bluetooth low energy APIs, Room DB for on-phone data persistence and source of truth.

Safety-critical workflows for alarm delivery and reliable background execution are implemented directly against native iOS SDK and Android SDK APIs.
DI-DO ROW 10 | 1: DI-293 | 2: APP-SRS-6.1.7 | 3: UN-102 Device Support | 4: DI-8 | 5: 293 | 6: 293 | 7: 655 | 8: Locally persisted data must be performant over the intended lifespan, noting the continual data generated by the CGM. | 9: Data Persistence Performance Under Continuous CGM Operation | 10: Glucose measurement history is stored locally using very mature and performant database systems, Core Data and Room DB on iOS and Android platforms respectively.

All data retrieval is scoped by date range or session identifier, and user identifier before loading into memory. Full-store loads for a single screen do not occur as the date range filter have an upper limit and are always applied.

Large data window fetches (30-day and 90-day report queries) are dispatched off the main thread and any rapid queries (single row tables) executed synchronously where possible to improve thread safety.

Chart components on both platforms receive pre-aggregated data as input to provide charting libraries on each platform with bounded input sizes per rendering frame.

DI-DO ROW 12 | 3: UN-102 Device Support | 4: DI-10 | 5: 271 | 6: 271 | 7: 657 | 8: The application must avoid initiating operating system limits and usage throttling (e.g. Ble scan throttling, wake lock overuse), so that the application continues to function reliably over time, and while running in the background. | 9: iOS Background Execution and OS Limit Compliance | 10: Undocumented wake mechanisms, busy-wait loops, and continuous unbounded BLE scans are not used, ensuring the application remains within background execution limits.

On iOS, the application maintains continuous BLE connectivity during device sleep using the "bluetooth-central" background mode, declared in "UIBackgroundModes" in "Info.plist". All background BLE work is performed via CoreBluetooth delegate callbacks where background wake timers are bounded and notification delivery uses standard iOS notification APIs.

On Android Ble scanning is not performed continuously for device reconnection to avoid initiating operating system limits and throttling which would result in no devices found after some time. The native Bluetooth API "automatic" reconnect parameter is utilised so the system understands the application is searching for a device, and will perform timely wakes during sleep mode after 15-30 minutes. Wake locks are only ever utilised with appropriate timeouts, and consider the deep sleep interval of 15-30 minutes to prevent overuse in a 24 hour period. Continuous BLE operation is supported by a Foreground Service, where a connectedDevice type is declared in "AndroidManifest.xml" to help prevent operating system limits being applied. The application also ensures the user has configured the system to avoid battery optimisations being applied to the application specifically, which also helps prevent operating system limits being applied. | 11: if iOS terminates the application during a low-memory event while backgrounded, the BLE session is not automatically restored on next launch, as CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey is not currently configured

DI-DO ROW 32 | 1: DI-273 | 2: APP-SRS-5.1.11 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-30 | 5: 302 | 6: 302 | 7: 676 | 8: All manual or automated data ingestion from untrusted sources (user / third party) must be validated for accuracy and consistency | 10: Email format, phone number format, and password policy rules are enforced locally by Keycloak registration within both the iOS and Android applications. All numeric fields for manual journal entries (insulin, activity, carbohydrate, medication) use bounded input controls rather than free-text fields, with limits set appropriately for the unit in question. Free text fields are always length-limited appropriately. Date and time pickers for manual entries are capped to on or before the current datetime and no older than 1 week using trusted time validation where cached / retried successfully at time of entry, or using local untrusted time when trusted time is still not available. To permit offline creation of events, additional backend driven validation by trusted time modules is applied when the event is uploadede, and any issue with the record validation results in deletion of the locally held invalid record (at the first opportunity).

Data ingestion from Google health and Apple health are validation as within realistic limits per day or discarded.

Push notifications are treated as untrusted and potentially received out-of-band or relating to a different user. They are only utilised to restart the application if it has been killed and was unable to restart by itself.

System generated BLE events are only ever received from trusted system sources.

BLE calibration values are verified as within an appropriate range for calibration, and the time utilised for the calibration is also ensured to be accurate.

Untrusted system sources of callbacks or events (which may be initiated by other malicious applications) are always avoided if possible, or validated, or configured to have no application impact.

DI-DO ROW 39 | 1: DI-293 | 2: APP-SRS-6.1.7 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-37 | 5: 312 | 6: 312 | 7: 683 | 8: The application must be architected to reduce the likelihood of coding errors for one feature impacting other parts of the system (i.e. separating unrelated data into separate tables, data structured to separate read only data from regularly mutated data) | 9: Application Architecture for Feature Isolation | 10: The application partitions data and processing by feature domain so that defects in one workflow are contained within that workflow’s storage, business rules, and synchronization path.

Persistent data is separated into distinct entities for independently owned domains such as authentication/session state, user profile, device and sensor session records, glucose measurements, calibration records, alerts and notifications, sharing, reporting/export, and queued upload operations.

Frequently mutated operational data is kept separate from read-only or rarely changed reference/configuration data, and derived or presentation-specific data is stored separately from source clinical records so that reporting, export, or UI defects do not overwrite the underlying measurement history.

State based design is utilised for the majority of the design so that the state of the application is always available and can be checked and validated and asserted in all conditions and combinations of conditions, and so that coding errors don't result in missed or incorrectly processed temporary events.

Each feature is implemented behind its own boundary, with typed models and feature-specific validation, mapping, and persistence logic. Presentation layers call these feature interfaces rather than reading and writing unrelated tables or shared mutable structures directly. Cross-feature interaction occurs only through defined contracts, such as identifiers, normalized domain models, or event notifications, instead of by allowing one feature to manipulate another feature’s internal storage.

Background sync, migration, and cache refresh routines operate on their own owned data sets and write scopes, with transactions limited to the affected domain.

The application database is treated as the ultimate source of truth, with transactions to ensure consistency through any errors. Domain specific singletons are utilised where possible to prevent potential threading issues and duplication of data is avoided where possible (including additional copies of derived data). | 11: Source of truth needs to be mentioned

This is not particularly about persistence (ignore the examples), we have another DI for that

Talk about state based architecture to prevent concurrency issues when mutating the data
DI-DO ROW 40 | 1: DI-293 | 2: APP-SRS-6.1.7 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-38 | 5: 313 | 6: 313 | 7: 684 | 8: Locally persisted data must utilise coding features to reduce maintenance cost and risk of introducing inadvertent errors (e.g. non-null fields) | 9: Typed Persistence Accessors and Shared Mappers | 10: Each functional domain is stored in its own dedicated entity or table. Read-only reference data (CGM measurement data received from the transmitter, and manual journal entries) are stored separately from regularly mutated data (notification records, user settings).

The persistence layer uses platform-native typed data access mechanisms to reduce maintenance cost and the risk of introducing inadvertent data errors, with field mapping, unit conversion, and validation being centralised in a reusable manner. On Android, Room data classes provide typed field access with compile-time verification.

Non-null constraints are applied at the schema level on both platforms for fields where null values would represent a data integrity failure and foreign keys are used with the appropriate cascade setting to ensure data consistency across multiple tables. Transactions are utilised to prevent concurrent modifications from resulting in data errors when multiple fields or tables are being updated simultaneously and to prevent inconsistency after power loss or crash.

In memory caches are preferred over disk caches to prevent long-lived cache errors.
DI-DO ROW 41 | 1: DI-293 | 2: APP-SRS-6.1.7 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-39 | 5: 314 | 6: 314 | 7: 685 | 8: The application must ensure atomicity of changes when multiple locally persisted data fields are updated at once (e.g. in response to a single triggering event or user interaction), to prevent corruption if the application is terminated during the persist operation. | 9: Atomic Writes for Multi-Field Updates | 10: Related field updates originating from the same protocol event or user action are committed within a single transaction boundary, ensuring they succeed (or fail together). DI-DO ROW 47 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-45 | 5: 320 | 6: 320 | 7: 690 | 8: Graphs with a time axis must ensure data points are plotted by timestamp and not other database or measurement indexes, to ensure the values position correctly between the axis labels and are displayed in a true linear progression over time. (e.g. not just equally spaced points) | 9: Timestamp-Based Chart X-Axis | 10: On both iOS and Android, the chart data construction layer uses the trusted CGM measurement creation timestamp as the X-axis value for all glucose history and AGP charts. The value is trusted because the session start time is verified and cannot change, and transmitter indexes are used to derive the measurement timestamp from this trusted session start time. This design prevents misleading visual compression or expansion of time intervals that would occur if data points were equally spaced regardless of their actual temporal distribution.

All time-series chart entries are positioned on the X-axis by absolute measurement timestamp for linearity (UTC epoch), not by database row ID, record index, or measurement sequence number. Data points are sorted by timestamp before chart data is constructed to remove any risk of misdisplay due to unwanted SOUP behaviour.

The graph bounds are configured to display up to and including all data points. This includes data points in the future according to the untrusted user phone time (the untrusted user phone time can be incorrect or there can be some limited transmitter drift into the future).
DI-DO ROW 48 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-46 | 5: 321 | 6: 321 | 7: 691 | 8: Rounding of any floating point values must be consistent and reduce the risk of human error for data storage, algorithm, and display purposes. | 9: Floating Point Rounding Consistency | 10: Rounding of glucose values is applied consistently across all data paths, storage, algorithm input, and display to prevent inconsistent representations of the same glucose value appearing on different screens.

The application and backend architecture stores glucose data in a single unit consistently, mg/dL, as it is reported from the transmitter to minimise the number of possible conversions, and other manual user input types fixed as well.

Mmol/L values are always rounded the nearest one decimal place and mg/dL values are always rounded to the nearest integer. A single formatting path determines the rounding precision based on the user's configured unit of measure, and this formatting path is applied uniformly across dashboard displays, chart axis labels, chart data points, and notification content.
DI-DO ROW 49 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-47 | 5: 322 | 6: 322 | 7: 692 | 8: The application must not be unduly affected by incorrect system date, time or timezone | 9: Clock-Independent System Behaviour | 10: All clinical timestamps are stored and transmitted in UTC (millis, or seconds, or ISO 8601 format), making persistence independent of the device's local timezone setting and any user manipulation of the system clock.

The application trusted time module is used to warn the user with specific UI when the trusted time module is available and a discrepancy (+- 180 seconds) is detected / their local phone device time/timezone appears to be incorrect on:
* Session start - preventing the start.
* inputting events - preventing the entry.
* phone time/timezone change - through medium priority notification timestamped with the trusted time.

Note:
* If a discrepancy continues to remain unresolved and alarms or notifications are generated, any timestamps used for these in the journal or persisted in the database must be directly from the trusted time.
* Calibration does not utilise timestamps but sends the blood glucose measurement immediately to the transmitter to be applied from the next measurement index (if stable / accepted by the transmitter), and the application also ensures the provided measurement is not too old (due to waiting on the calibration screen before submitting).

Session start times are stored as UTC epoch values, and validated at the moment of creation with trusted time modules, with one exception where the user needs to start a session offline and the trusted time module is unavailable for this reason, in which case the untrusted phone time must be used but the user is asked to manually confirm the time/timezone is correct before proceeding. The BLE command layer on both platforms uses the trusted session start time, not the current phone clock, when deriving measurement timestamps. Note the session start time is stored in the transmitter and cannot be changed for the duration of the session and is retrieved and confirmed against the locally held value of session start time (along with transmitter, session index, etc.), avoiding any possible persistence or sync issues, and providing for offline derivation.

The application validates timestamps to ensure user events are never created in the future or too far in the past according to the local phone time, and the user will see an error message preventing the event from being saved if the phone time/timezone is detected to be incorrect during this validation. In the case where events are being created offline and the trusted time module is unavailable for any reason the user's local phone time is trusted temporarily until event upload when it is validated for obvious inconsistency by the backend. If the backend rejects the event due to it being timestamped too far in the future, the event is removed from the local data store of the application and the user is notified with a medium priority notification. | 11: No NTP or server-clock offset calculation is implemented on either platform. If the user manually sets an incorrect system time before the first server sync, measurements taken during that window carry incorrect UTC timestamps. The design requires a trusted time source (network time or server timestamp at session start) to anchor all clinical timestamp generation. The current implementation requires remediation.

DI-DO ROW 64 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-62 | 5: 342 | 6: 342 | 7: 706 | 8: Once the CGM is active, the application must remain alive in the background or restart automatically without user interaction so that functionality is sufficiently continual. This should include multiple keep alive methods to maximise reliability. | 9: CGM Session Background Monitoring Keep-Alive | 10: Once a CGM session is active, the application remains operational in the background and restarts automatically after termination, without requiring user interaction. Multiple keep-alive methods are employed in combination to maximise reliability, because the mobile operating system aggressively optimises applications and is well known to terminate or suspend them.

On iOS, complementary keep-alive methods are configured considering the three states (active - fully in memory and executing code, suspended - fully in memory but not executing code, terminated - ):
1) Enabling "run in background support", with a scheduled background task for periodic application refresh, with a requested rate of 300 seconds, executed at approximately 15-30 minutes by the operating system. If being used to restore the application from the terminated state, it will only be able to keep the application alive for a shorter time, approximately 5 minutes (and periodically). This does not help with the suspended state.
2) Active Bluetooth low energy connection (or active reconnection request), with bluetooth-central background mode. This helps prevent the suspended state and keep the app in the active state.
3) CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey allows iOS to relaunch the app after it was terminated so Bluetooth activity can continue. This will trigger when coming back into Bluetooth range from a disconnected CGM.
4) "Silent" push notifications dispatched from the backend during a session (external to the application) prevent the application from remaining in the suspended state indefinitely.
5) "Noisy" push notifications dispatched from the backend during a session (external to the application) if the backend has not received session data for the last 30 minutes, to encourage the user to re-open the application from a terminated state when other mechanisms have failed (interactivity is required.

On Android, complementary keep-alive methods are configured considering the two states (active - fully in memory and executing code, terminated - no memory and no code execution):
1) Android foreground service with the connected-device service type and ongoing notification, helps the operating system understand the application is required for the ongoing CGM session and should not be terminated.
2) Companion device manager is utilised for the bluetooth pairing which creates an additional "association" with the operating system, which makes application death less likely and the application configures an OS-level service which registers to receive associated "device appeared" callbacks, which can bring the application back from a terminated state.
3) The user is guided to and must configure the application battery optimisation exemption request, mitigating certain application doze and standby restrictions.
4) Android job service registers the application for periodic pings at approximately a 15 minute period (the fastest available). This is able to persist after application death and restarts the application if necessary.
5) The application registers with the system for startup after phone reboot. On some mobile phones this requires an additional permission / user configuration, which the application aims to prompt as required (but note there is no official API for this, so it is a heuristic). If the boot receiver is not executed the other mechanisms would be used.
6) Push notifications dispatched from the backend (external to the application) bring the application back alive from a terminated state when other mechanisms have failed.
7) Direct boot no-data alarm notifies the user if the application did not fully restart due to the phone not fully restarting. | 11: iOS does not configure BLE state restoration during CoreBluetooth central manager initialisation. Without this, the BLE session may not survive iOS terminating the application under memory pressure. The application must be updated to enable CoreBluetooth state restoration.

DI-DO ROW 70 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-68 | 5: 348 | 6: 348 | 7: 712 | 8: The application must not persist or utilise any received measurements, and must not send any requests for missing readings, and must not send any session modification commands, until it has verified the transmitter serial number, firmware version, and session index match the expected session. If it cannot verify due to missing or mismatched cryptographic credentials, it may perform the challenge procedure first. | 9: Pre-Measurement Session Verification | 10: Before the application persists any received measurements, sends any RACP requests, or issues any session modification commands, it verifies that the transmitter, firmware version and session are as expected. It is noted that the process of firmware update is only performed outside of a session because it is utilises the same flash where measurements are stored. (In development it is possible to update boards without this limitation so the code is written to handle and support it either way).

Delayed persistence until verification of transmitter serial (A), firmware version (A), expected active session identifier, expected active session start time:
After every bluetooth connection is initiated (and on each re-connection), the Modus state machine initialises from scratch. Measurements are not persisted until one of a number of data accepting states have been reached. Before these states have been reached, to save re-transmission via RACP later, a list of received measurement-specific data packets (encrypted and unparsed) are stored in memory as long as the correct transmitter remains connected until the application has completed the verification process, at which point it attempts to decrypt and persist them:
1) The state machine first executes the device info command and verifying the returned transmitter serial number matches the expected session persisted locally, and verifying the returned firmware version is within a range supported by the application. A mismatch moves to a terminal error state.
2) The state machine then executes the device status command and verifying the returned state is IN_PROGRESS to proceed towards the data accepting states. A mismatch moves one of the "session ended" terminal states.
3) The state machine then verifies the transmitter specific AES key is available, and if not, performs the key challenge procedure before proceeding.
4) The state machine then executes the in progress session info command and verifying the returned session index and returned session start time matches the expected session data persisted locally. A mismatch moves to the "session ended" terminal state. This command is also executed with the optional encrypted=true flag, which allows the app to get an immediate response indicating if the app's stored AES key is incorrect (rather than waiting for the next data packet decrypt operation or RACP request to fail).
5) The state machine then moves to one of the data accepting states (including a state which utilises RACP commands if necessary), and immediately processes any measurement packets which were buffered during the state machine initialisation flow before proceeding.

Delayed persistence until verification of transmitter serial (B):
* Before any modification commands or received health data can be utilised, the application must have the correct AES key to encrypt and decrypt command payloads for the Modus application-layer encryption (this is in addition to Bluetooth communication encryption). This is the first implicit step of transmitter verification, because the AES key persisted in the app is transmitter-unique and generated by the backend with a challenge process to guarantee the transmitter is genuine. The app negotiates this key before utilising the transmitter, or re-negotiates it if there is an error in decryption, and it is persisted locally against transmitter serial number thereby implicitly verifying it. Note that some simple commands such as device info and device status are not encrypted, but all health information has the encryption applied.

Delayed persistence until verification of firmware version (B):
* The application requires and checks for a specific UUID associated with the supported firmware version(s). Modus protocol is to update the UUID used by transmitter firmware on breaking API changes. If the firmware has been updated with breaking changes and the application is outdated, it simply will not communicate with the new firmware, so no transmitter commands will be executed, and no measurements will be received or persisted.
DI-DO ROW 71 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-69 | 5: 349 | 6: 349 | 7: 713 | 8: The critical low glucose alarm threshold must be set appropriately and the threshold is not user configurable. | 9: Fixed Critical Low Glucose Alarm Threshold | 10: The critical low alarm threshold is not user configurable for safety and is fixed in the application to 56 mg/dL (any display-only rendering of the thresold itself will be in the user's glucose unit). User calibrations are also implemented in such a way that there is no safety impact on this critical low glucose threshold, only values above the threshold are permitted to be modified by manual user calibrations, and the calibrations can never be applied such that a value above the critical low glucose threshold is reduced into it (to prevent nuisance alarms impacting the trust and genuine severity of this alarm). | 11: This DO records the design for DI-69 (fixed, non-user-configurable urgent-low threshold). DI-DO ROW 72 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-70 | 5: 365 | 6: 365 | 7: 714 | 8: Once stopped by a user, the critical low glucose alarm must automatically become enabled again after an appropriate period of time, and will therefore re-activate if the low condition is still present | 9: Critical Low Alarm Auto-Re-Arm After Snooze | 10: When the user stops the critical low glucose alarm, it is performed as a "snooze" function. Snooze only allows fixed selection of potential snooze durations, up to 1 hour. The alarm will become enabled after the snooze duration expires, without any user input.

After snooze is elapsed / disabled, manually or automatically, immediately on receipt of the next real-time non-RACP measurement from a CGM (up to 1 minute later), the alarm will re-trigger as normal if the low glucose condition is still present.

The snooze delay is timed by in-memory elapsed monotonic clocktime (which increases regardless of CPU sleep), for reliability against incorrect device time and regardless of trusted time availability offline. This means that if the application is terminated or restarts during snooze, the behaviour is fail-safe and the snooze period is cancelled and the critical low alarm can sound again when the next realtime measurement arrives if the low condition persists.

This reliance on real-time measurements is to ensure safe-by-design behaviour that ensures this alarm is not based off of untrusted device time to determine the "freshness" of the last received measurement which may or may not be realtime any more. Incorrect device time could potentially be an issue when the trusted time cache is not available (e.g. offline usage after phone or application restart).

If the CGM has stopped delivering real-time readings, user communication of this is handled through the no-data alarm specified in other requirements.

If a new measurement arrives above the critical low threshold while the alarm is snoozed, the snooze period continues counting down (rather than resetting) to prevent nuisance alarms if the measurements are cycling above and below the threshold.

If the session ends with explicit user confirmation while the alarm is snoozed, then the snooze (and any active critical low alarm) is reset / cleared ready for the user's next session.

DI-DO ROW 77 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 4: DI-75 | 5: 375 | 6: 375 | 7: 719 | 8: All real-time and historical glucose measurements must be timestamped such that they are resilient to wrong times from the untrusted system phone time setting. Note the untrusted system phone time setting can be changed at any time by the user or automatic location/network adjustments. | 9: Trusted Timestamp for Glucose Measurement and Display | 10: All CGM glucose timestamps are derived from the sensor session start time, which is stored in UTC, making them independent of the device's local timezone setting. The session start time is stored in the transmitter at the moment of session start, as a UTC epoch value and used as the temporal anchor for all measurements within that session, as they are derived from the start time and the measurement index. The session start time is fetched through Bluetooth via the get session info command at runtime by the Modus application, and validated against the locally persisted value for the "expected session start time" (along with the expected session ID), before any index derivations are made by the app.

All display and interpretation of these trusted measurement timestamps apply timezone localisation at render time only, ensuring that the stored data is timezone-neutral and the displayed representation adapts to the user's current setting.

Once written to a transmitter the session start time is considered a trusted value, and because it is only written to the transmitter once and impacts all measurement timestamps, additional effort is placed to ensure this trust. Both iOS and Android implement trusted time modules which synchronise with the internet, and compare a trusted server time with the local phone time, ensuring a deviation of no more than +- 180 seconds before utilising any phone time value. This also provides a secondary benefit of notifying the user if their device time or timezone is incorrectly configured which impacts some other application features, and attempting to force the user to resolve these issues before session start.

To meet the requirement that sensor sessions must be startable while the user does not have internet connection, the apps attempt to maintain a long-lived trusted time cache  from the last successful API call, which can estimate a trusted server time from each device's internal monotonic clock, time since boot, this is available as long as the phone or application is not restarted. The trusted time modules are also utilised for interrupted session resume, which requires the current time to be sent to the transmitter.

Due to potential monotonic clock drift of the trusted time cache and the trusted server time including a network latency element, the server time is only used for the deviation check and the untrusted phone time is the actual utilised value when within acceptable tolerance (phone time is less likely to drift than our cache when correct).

If the trusted time cache is not available for session start or resume (e.g. offline usage after application restart), the user must still be able to start a new CGM sensor session, and is prompted to manually confirm the time and timezone is correct.

The snapshot used for time derivation attempts to update periodically every 60 minutes if internet is available, and also attempts to update during the new session flow (and the UI waits for this additional re-check). This periodic refresh and refresh during the new session flow is necessary as the monotonic clocks do drift with device deep sleep, lock screen activity and charging, so are only used to validate the user's untrusted phone time is within 180 seconds of the estimated server time. | 11: No NTP synchronisation or server-time offset correction is implemented on either platform. Timestamps are generated from the device system clock at the moment of measurement. If the user's device clock is incorrect, the UTC timestamp stored will also be incorrect.

This DI requires a trusted timestamp source. The design requires that the session start time be anchored to a server-confirmed UTC time, and that subsequent measurement timestamps be computed relative to that anchor using the transmitter's elapsed-time counter rather than the phone clock.

DI-DO ROW 80 | 7: 732 | 8: Linked to 302 / 311 / 322 / 340 / 352 / 355 / 375 / 377 / 445 / 446 / 447 / 448 / 449 / 720 / 721 / 728 / 730 / 733 / 769 / 772 / 815 / 832 / 837 /  | 9: Trusted Time Module | 10: Trusted date/time component with cache:
Note the requirement to be able to start a new sensor session offline if at all possible, for this reason the trusted date/time component has a cache which allows verification of the user's phone time and timezone while internet access is unavailable. Internet access is used to fetch a trusted server time snapshot from the backend (applying a small compensation estimate for half round trip latency), and "snapshotting" this alongside a value of the mobile phone's uptime since last boot (a monotonically increasing clock counter). Once this snapshot is made, it is kept in memory cache, and it can be used offline for a "derived trusted server time", as uptime since boot is available offline and provides the delta time since snapshot. The "derived trusted server time" is trusted, but potentially drifted, so it is ideally not used directly (unless the application has no other choice), but ideally only used to validate the local phone time is within acceptable +- 180 second tolerance. The snapshot is only retained in memory as it becomes completely invalid if the system reboots, after which the monotonic clock snapshot for uptime since last phone boot is invalid.

Every time the trusted time component is used to validate local time and the validation fails, a low priority notification is sent to the user as a reminder to fix their device.

Note:
Server time is preferred as incorrect time+timezone may be invisible to the user while the displayed clock can still appear correct but will any programmatic time APIs will report incorrect UTC time. This condition is most common after the user has been travelling internationally and attempted to manually set the device time to appear correct and compensate for an incorrectly manually set timezone.

Offline trusted date/time cache availability depends on:
    (i) Internet connection for a trusted server time from the backend. An empty cache retries a fetch periodically every 30 minutes. Initial fetch performed on application startup.
    (ii) The snapshot was refreshed with successful internet access (periodically every 2 hours after last successful snapshot), for a new trusted server snapshot without any drift.
    (iii) Cache age not exceeding 15 days (measured by monotonic cache clock), to match the session length for one sensor and to not have excessive drift exceeding the +- 3 minute validation window. Old cache is cleared so the user must be online at least once in every 15 days to avoid the manual time check.
    (iv) The trusted time component was able to retain the cached snapshot in memory, which requires the application remain alive.
    (v) The trusted time component was able to restore a snapshot into memory cache after an application restart, only if the phone operating system did not restart. 
   (vi) The application being actively involved in a CGM session so that its process is more likely to remain alive, note that the trusted time cache is also utilised outside of a session and for session start and for this reason offlline usage is important as it may be quite unreliable outside of an active session.

Note that for the following reasons the transmitter expiry date is not extracted from the GS1 barcode on transmitter packaging or the transmitter itself via an in-app camera feature, but fetched from the backend and based on the transmitter serial number which the CGM reports through the Bluetooth connection:
1) Sensor packaging is different from transmitter packaging, and due to the reusable nature of the transmitter, it is assumed the user will have discarded the transmitter packaging after first use.
2) Once the transmitter is attached to a sensor the barcode printed on the transmitter is face down and inaccessible.
2) Once the transmitter is attached to a sensor (required to start receiving power and connect), even if there was an outer barcode it would likely be physically out of reach on the back of an arm for the user in terms of barcode scanning with a camera.

Safe by design - The first time a transmitter is used in the application (or after app data clear), it must have an internet connection to negotiate the transmitter encryption keys with the backend. These keys are persisted and unique to each transmitter registration, and the application also fetches the transmitter expiry date from the backend, and persists it alongside the encryption key. When the encryption key is cleared due to app reinstall or data deletion, internet connection is required again to re-register for another encryption key, so the expiration date will always be available alongside the verified genuine transmitter encryption key without fail. | 11: needs implementation
DI-DO ROW 83 | 1: DI-311 | 2: APP-SRS-6.3.9 | 3: UN-100 Traceable Components | 4: DI-79 | 5: 311 | 6: 311 | 7: 735 | 8: The user must be prompted to apply critical firmware updates to their transmitter, checked immediately before starting a new session (because the firmware cannot be updated mid-way into a session), and be forbidden from proceeding until an update can complete safely and without compatibility concerns. | 9: Pre-Session Firmware Version Check | 10: FIRMWARE CRITICAL UPDATES (AT SESSION START):
(Shared base recall/update fetch and persistence logic): The application polls the server on application startup and then opens a gRPC stream to receive real-time updates to the firmware recall notices / critical update version mappings (update mapping must be optional in case the recall needs to be made before firmware update is available). The stream reconnects as soon as network becomes available with gRPC streaming behaviour. If a mandatory firmware update is pending, the user is directed to the firmware update process, which is a dismissable firmware update screen, and download/install begins immediately without user intervention or confirmation. The firmware is downloaded and applied as long as the transmitter remains connected. Any failure to download prompts the user to retry. The user must always have the option to leave the download/install screen to prevent usage of historical glucose data and in case a system error is rendering the transmitter unusable and access to customer support information is required. If the transmitter disconnects the download continues until complete in the background (singleton implementation), even if the user exits (and the downloaded file persists in the application-secure directory to speed up the update process on the next connection). If the transmitter disconnects the user is returned to the BLE scanning/pairing screen with the usual error where they can retry the connection.

A state machine tracks progress through starting, uploading, and completed phases. On successful completion, after the new firmware version is re-checked and confirmed through the transmitter API, the blocking state is cleared and the session start flow is permitted. | 11: needs implementation

There is no blocking functionality based on the age of the recall cache for offline usage, however the application attempts to call the recall API to refresh the persisted recall notices at the moment it is needed during the session start flow (in additional to the other checks), awaiting the result but proceeding regardless of refresh outcome for offline usage.

Before a session is started, the application matches the transmitter's serial number (obtained via BLE after transmitter connection) or batch ID (obtained via backend API for transmitter registration along with the transmitter encryption key) against the locally persisted recall list. A recall blocks the user from completing the session start flow and the user is informed of a recall.

During an active session, receipt of an updated recall list that includes the current transmitter triggers an immediate critical severity recall alarm to the user so they are aware, which can be snoozed for up to 8 hours (to allow the user to continue their session and sleep), and will sound again after this time. There is no limit on the number of snoozes and the application does not forbid (potentially invalid) continual measurements, but the critical alarm ensures the user is continually aware for the remainder of their session. | 11: needs implementation

The database encryption key is securely persisted and protected as an encrypted entity in the application's private location (sandbox). DI-DO ROW 94 | 1: DI-293 | 2: APP-SRS-6.1.7 | 3: UN-101 Security & Confidentiality | 4: DI-89 | 5: 454 | 6: 454 | 7: 727 | 8: The application must be architected to ensure data cannot suffer any query/prompt injection from untrusted input (e.g. user submitted fields). | 9: Query Injection Prevention for Local Data Access | 10: All local database queries use parameterised, typed query mechanisms that enforce structural separation between query logic and data values. DI-DO ROW 104 | 3: UN-101 Security & Confidentiality | 4: DI-99 | 5: 464 | 6: 464 | 7: 745 | 8: Secure and remotely verified user authentication must be required to access personal data | 9: Authenticated Access to Personal Data | 10: Access to PHI-displaying screens including the glucose dashboard, logbook, reports, and settings requires a valid, server-verified authentication session. DI-DO ROW 105 | 3: UN-101 Security & Confidentiality | 4: DI-100 | 5: 465 | 6: 465 | 7: 746 | 8: The application must ensure confidentiality of all user data during Bluetooth transmission. | 9: BLE Encryption | 10: The BLE protocol layer itself is utilised for encrypted communication and integrity checking.

In addition to the BLE layer, Modus application layer encryption and integrity checking is implemented when protected commands and PII is in question: On initial transmitter registration, the embedded Firmware generates a cryptographically random registration challenge and transmits it to the iOS/Android app. The app forwards this and the device serial number to the Backend API. The Backend retrieves the device's unique 128-bit Device Root Key (DRK) without the app ever receiving it, generates its own challenge response, and derives a 128-bit session key. The app forwards the challenge response to the embedded firmware for it to verify the backend has validated the transmitter, but does not forward the session key so that no third party in the middle can decrypt the encrypted dealth data or run protected commands on the transmitter. The apps also ensure unique nonce usage for every command payload that is sent to the transmitter. The session key is persisted in the app as long as possible so that future sessions can be started with the same transmitter offline. Note the transmitter is able to derive the same SessionKey using the same HKDF inputs the server utilised (the same DRK is kept private in the transmitter). The DRK never traverses the BLE channel or internet channel. The iOS/Android app does not possess the DRK and cannot derive the SessionKey independently. Any tampered packets are detected and discarded at the recipient's authentication tag verification step.

DI-DO ROW 107 | 3: UN-101 Security & Confidentiality | 4: DI-102 | 5: 467 | 6: 467 | 7: 748 | 8: Bluetooth denial of service vulnerabilities must be minimised as much as possible, noting the user must understand limitations and be able to recreate the device pairing mid-way through the session. | 9: BLE Denial-of-Service Resilience and User Recovery | 10: BLE radio jamming and forced disconnection through RF interference are physical-layer attacks the iOS/Android app cannot prevent, though many mitigations are implemented at the firmware level.

The app's contribution to DoS resilience is therefore limited to: 
 - remaining connected to the transmitter as reliably as possible during an active session, and reconnecting as fast as possible, to prevent the firmware accepting any other potentially malicious connection.
 - ensuring measurements recorded by the embedded firmware during any disconnected period are retrieved from transmitter storage on reconnection, so the data gap in the session record is minimised.
 - clear user interface surrounding user-initiated disconnection from a transmitter for the phone change procedure and associated 30 minute "cooldown" which is enforced by the firmware.
 - automatically disconnecting from the transmitter immediately from terminal error states (failed sensor) where the user might want to utilise a different phone for the next session. | 11: While the application is connected to a transmitter, the transmitter will not advertise nearby. A different phone cannot connect to the transmitter within 30 minutes of a disconnection event. This is a balanced limitation between allowing the pairing to be changed mid-session (so that a user can change phone or repair a damaged connection after unexpected behaviour), and how quickly a transmitter would be connectable to by a malicious actor, and also the length of time the mobile operating system may "pause" the app's Bluetooth connection during deep sleep while the phone is not in use (typically 15-25 minutes).

Any malicious actor would need to remain in physical proximity to continually prevent the user from receiving further readings.

Any malicious actor would not be able to access any health data collected during the denial of service, and it would remain available to the user once the connection to thei

The app attempts to remain connected at all times while a session is running. It also attempts to disconnect as soon as possible after a terminal session or error state to prevent self-denial of service in case the user changes phone due to problems with the session or transmitter.
DI-DO ROW 108 | 3: UN-101 Security & Confidentiality | 4: DI-103 | 5: 468 | 6: 468 | 8: Shared data must allow the user to specify data types which will not be shared. | 9: Sharing Relationship and Data Type Configuration | 10: The app supports two sharing relationship types: user-to-user (e.g., family member or carer) and user-to-HCP. Both are established via an invitation flow managed by the Backend. The sharing permission model is opt-in per data type and no categories are shared by default. When establishing or modifying a sharing relationship, the user selects which data type categories the recipient may view. The available categories include at minimum glucose measurements, insulin records, carbohydrate intake and activity data.

The app does not transmit health data directly to sharing recipients. All recipient data access is mediated by the Backend in accordance with the permissions configured by the data-owner user. When the data-owner modifies permissions for an active relationship, the change is submitted to the Backend via an authenticated API call. The Backend enforces the updated permissions immediately and the data types the user has deselected are no longer accessible to the recipient from that point forward. If the change was not possible due to server error or network error, the user is informed immediately with error messaging. Previously visible data of a deselected type is not retroactively surfaced after the permission change takes effect.
DI-DO ROW 109 | 3: UN-101 Security & Confidentiality | 4: DI-104 | 5: 469 | 6: 469 | 8: OTP must be used for acceptance of a data-sharing invitation. | 9: OTP Verification for User-to-User Sharing Invitation Acceptance | 10: The data owner initiates the sharing invitation from the app. The Backend issues an OTP and delivers it out-of-band to the invitee via their verified email. The invitee opens the iOS/Android app on their own device, navigates to the pending invitation, and enters the received OTP. The app submits the OTP to the Portal Backend via an authenticated API call. The Backend validates the code against the pending invitation record by checking both value and expiry and returns success or failure. On success, the sharing relationship is activated and the invitee gains access to the data types configured by the data owner. On failure, the app presents an error state and the invitation remains inactive.

The OTP is not stored locally on the device beyond the active entry session and is not written to logs or crash reports.

The HCP initiates the data access request via the Portal or a separate HCP-facing channel. The Portal Backend issues an OTP and delivers it to the data owner via their verified email. The data owner opens the app on their own device, navigates to the pending HCP request, and enters the received OTP to approve it. The app submits the OTP to the Portal Backend via an authenticated API call. The Backend validates the code against the pending request record by checking both value and expiry and returns success or failure. On success, the HCP is granted access to the data types the data owner has configured. On failure, the app presents an error state and the request remains inactive.

After a new sensor session begins, the application is connected to the transmitter and displays the appropriate UI based on the state reported by the transmitter. This screen is displayed until the user leaves it, after which the dashboard CGM measurement panel shows that warm up is in progress (in place of a measurement value) and the estimated remaining warm-up time. Any Bluetooth interruption or disconnection will not disrupt/reset the stabilisation as it is firmware driven, and will continue to display if still warming-up after reconnection.

Safe by design: The CGM monitoring dashboard only shows glucose measurements from the current/expected CGM session and so it will never display a glucose value until the warm-up period has elapsed, as no glucose values are received from the transmitter until this is complete. 
DI-DO ROW 138 | 3: UN-105 Guidance | 4: DI-133 | 5: 717 | 6: 718 | 7: 821 | 8: If there is a continued interruption which would prevent the critical low glucose alarm from functioning for a medically significant period of time, the user must be informed at least once with a substantial alert visually and audibly equivalent to the alarm itself. Noting that mobile operating systems may deep-sleep applications overnight for substantial periods of time in approximately 15-30 minute intervals, and the user is likely to be asleep during these intervals. | 9: Critical Alarm Impairment Warning | 10: The no-data alarm is designed to operate from the same data source of truth (DO-849) as the critical low glucose alarm, to ensure full coverage across the combination of the no-data and the critical low glucose alarms (DO-835 / DO-864). Only the last expected measurement index impacts the no-data alarm as it relates to coverage for the critical low glucose alarm, fetching older measurements from RACP does not help the user if real-time measurements are missing. A triggered no-data alarm resets its snooze and sounding condition if the last expected measurement arrives again, unlike other critical alarms which continue until explicit user confirmation (noting that the last expected index continually increases as time elapses).

The no-data alarm is also designed to operate from the same data source of truth (DO-849) as the trend arrow calculation and the trend arrow rapidly falling / rising notifications, with additional behaviour relating to the measurements immediately before the latest index to ensure full coverage across the combination of the no-data alarm and the trend arrow notifications (notifications defined in DO-854). If the latest index is missing the no-data alarm will sound already to cover the loss of the critical low glucose alarm, the trend arrow calculation utilises the 14 measurements immeditely before the latest index (for a window with 15 measurements). The no-data alarm utilises the same constant that the trend component has to prevent accidental misalignment in future. The no-data alarm only ever raises a medium priority notification if any of the 14 rapidly falling or rising arrow related measurements are missing, as this the highest priority the rapidly falling / rapidly rising notifications are ever dispatched with.

There are multiple scenarios which prevent the critical low glucose alarm from functioning:
1) During remote monitoring measurements from another user - Internet connection is continually required.
2) Mobile phone hardware issues: Speaker / Amplifier malfunction, screen malfunction.
3) The uncontrolled nature of mobile phone operating systems and environments, where applications do not have the ability to fully control the phone or override certain user settings (Bluetooth enabled, Do not Disturb, notifications, lock screen security, speaker volume) because they run in a heavily sandboxed manner. This is further complicated by multiple versions of operating system as well as manufacturers customisation of the operating system environment so that there are a large variety of phone OS behaviours in circulation.
4) Reliance on the phone to continually maintain a Bluetooth connection: Mobile phone OS deep sleep periods sustaining periodic Bluetooth disconnects (usually while the phone is plugged in and charging). Note that the mobile phone updating or shutting down or restarting without the user unlocking after boot presents a scenario where the alarm or even notifications cannot function and the iOS application or CGM cannot react after-the-fact to this scenario, so the application attempts to warn the user of impending low phone battery in advance where possible.
5) Reliance on hardware to generate real-time measurements, which has a number of temporary or permanent interruption scenarios, sensor placement issues, physical sensor damage, physically applied pressure / torque, sensor chemistry lifetime, sensor battery issues. Permanent issues with the sensor are usually reported as failure states in the transmitter, but this is not assumed or guaranteed.
6) Reliance on real-time measurements continually arriving from the transmitter uninterrupted, including wireless connection interference, wireless range compromise, transmitter failure states, bluetooth disconnections.
7) Continual application permissions (note that the actual revoke action will terminate the application, but it should restart again afterwards), Bluetooth permission, 

DI-733 defines how the critical no-data alarm is resilient to application and phone restarts, including direct-boot-only partial phone restarts on Android.

The medium priority and escalated critical priority no-data alarm is used to cover any scenario where the critical low glucose alarm cannot function, other than entire phone shutdown which cannot be covered by any alarm - If the application is alive and has not received any recent measurement values (including measurement packets which arrived but without glucose values [this condition is suppressed until after warm-up], or glucose values which arrived but failed the application's sanity checks, or measurement packets which did not arrive at all for any reason) for the last 3 minutes / 3 measurement indexes (this time is purposely the same as the Bluetooth no-data state check after 3 minutes, as the usual outcome of this state check would be sensor failure), the no-data alarm is initiated.

The no-data alarm will begin as a medium priority alert and escalate to critical severity after a period of time, which is chosen initially based on how low the last glucose measurement was, and can be escalated immediately when the no-data is encountered at a relatively low glucose level. Escalation time is based on in-memory elapsed realtime as long as the application does not restart. If the application restarts the correct no-data escalation timer is restored with the correct remaining time, based on the trusted time module where possible, or untrusted phone time if not. This watchdog timer continues without erroneous reset even in a Bluetooth disconnecting and reconnecting cycle and/or remaining disconnected.

The medium priority no-data notification will pester the user every 15 minutes as long as the no-data issue remains unresolved. The critical no-data alarm is equivalent in volume and severity to the critical low glucose alarm. Critical no-data snooze is similar to the critical low glucose alarm, but tracked separately, permitting snooze up to 1 hour each time, with no upper limit on the number of snoozes. A snoozed no-data alarm cannot be reactivated early by direct user interaction through the settings like the critical low glucose alarm (to prevent confusion). Explicit user interaction is required with the same randomised location-press UI as the critical low glucose alarm. If the app is in the background, the UI will brought to the foreground when alarming in the exact same manner as the critical low glucose alarm.

The timing and glucose levels consider the following logic for designing against nuisance alarming:
* The patient usually begins sleep between 5-6 mmol/L, delay time until critical is considered as "time before waking an asleep user who did not notice the medium priority no-data alarm".
* The delay time is to allow the transmitter time to reconnect gracefully before sounding a critical alarm.
* The critical low glucose alarm threshold is fixed at 3.1 mmol/L.
* Android deep sleep disvonnects occur for approximately 15-35 minutes at a time, and so would inherently trigger the no-data alarm, escalation to critical priority during this period should be avoided if not necessary by utilising the last known glucose value to delay safely.
* A no-data scenario from a lower glucose value must escalate to critical sooner.
* A no-data scenario from a glucose value below 4.0 mmol/L must escalate immediately.
* A no-data scenario from a glucose value between 4.0 (inclusive) - 5.0 mmol/L (exclusive) must escalate after 0 - 22 minutes, determined linearly.
* A no-data scenario from a glucose value between 5.0 (inclusive) - 10.0 mmol/L (inclusive) must escalate after 37.5 - 90 minutes, determined linearly. This is a much longer delay than a scenario from glucose values below 5.0 mmol/L as it carries substantially less risk and so nuisance alarming can be prevented safely.
* A no-data scenario from a glucose value above 10.0 mmol/L must escalate after 90 minutes.

The system is designed to permit session initialisation offline as much as possible. The first-time transmitter registration must be performed online, after this offline ability is retained as long as the application database exists (the transmitter encryption key  is retained). The first-time CGM setup often immediately follows application download and user registration, and so internet access is expected. The sensor/transmitter session start procedure depends on the transmitter's current registration state which is held in the backend, and by extension the registration state held in the application:
* Transmitter not yet registered: The user must have internet access, and scan the GS1 barcode or manually enter the pairing PIN during the transmitter registration flow.
* Transmitter registered, app database holds empty or invalid key: The user must have internet access, no barcode scan is required.
* Transmitter registered, app database holds valid key: No internet access is required.

The system is designed to permit session initialisation offline as much as possible. Session start or resume usually depends on the availability of trusted time:
* Trusted time cache not available: No internet access is required, the user must confirm their local phone time is correct manually.
* Trusted time cache available: No internet access is required.

The sensor/transmitter session start procedure depends on the transmitter's current state which is fetched via Bluetooth after successful connection:
 * Session Stopped: Session start is initiated automatically. The application sends a StartSession command containing the trusted and verified start timestamp (seconds UTC), which was verified against server time or manually confirmed by the user. This trusted time is then persisted in the transmitter, and it is utilised to calculate trusted time values for each measurement based off measurement indexes (without utilising local user phone time, which can be incorrect). Session metadata is persisted locally on both platforms and reported to the backend.
 * Session In Progress, warming up / stabilising: A dedicated warmup progress screen is displayed, showing a progress indicator driven by estimated warmup remaining time. A warmup watchdog is in place: if the transmitter does not complete the warm up by the 3h mark (measured by transmitter index, essentially trusted time), the application will inform the user the sensor has failed and direct them to replace it. The measurement activity watchdog is armed: if the transmitter is connected but no new index is received within 3 minutes on an active session, the session status command is used to determine the actual state (in case the transmitter moves to failed or unknown states). RACP data recovery is performed for any missing indexes. The no-data alarm will not trigger based on lack of glucose values.
 * Session In Progress: The application navigates to the dashboard and begins receiving valid measurements. The measurement activity watchdog is armed: if the transmitter is connected but no new measurement is received within 3 minutes on an active session, the session status command is used to determine the actual state (in case the transmitter moves to failed or unknown states). RACP data recovery is performed for any missing measurements.
 * Session Completed: RACP data recovery is performed for any missing measurements, then the user is directed to replace their sensor. The power interruption of sensor replacement will transition the transmitter from the completed state to the stopped state (not the interrupted state).
 * Session Interrupted: This is usually caused by the user replacing their sensor early, without using the application UI to do so and cleanly shut down the previous session. The user is asked whether they have applied a new sensor or whether the application should continue with the existing sensor, and either aborts or resumes the existing session in response.
 * Session Failed / Unknown: Sensor replacement guidance is shown. | 11: Needs to be implemented
