DI-DO ROW 149 | 3: UN-123 CGM Session Management | 4: DI-141 | 5: 723 | 6: 725 | 7: 840 | 8: The user must be able to change mobile phone or recover from lost/invalidated Bluetooth pairing mid-way through a session, without removing the sensor, and without undue delay to receiving measurements on the new device. | 9: Phone Change and BLE Pairing Recovery Mid-Session | 10: Bluetooth pairing itself is stored and maintained by the operating system, it may be unexpectedly or intentionally removed outside of the application either by the phone user or by the operating system, and it will become no longer functional if a different device has connected and paired to the transmitter more recently than the phone in question.

Previously paired transmitter information including the Modus encryption AES key (required for offline use) is stored in the mobile application database. If the mobile application is uninstalled or the data is cleared it will be lost, or if the user has re-registered the transmitter from a different phone/app install (thereby setting up a new AES key) the old key will become invalid on the old phone. The application retains keys for multiple transmitters simultaneously for offline use, though the user is only able to connect to a single transmitter at a time through the application UI.

If the app data is not erased and the Modus transmitter encryption key is still valid, regardless of Bluetooth pairing loss, a re-pairing can be performed without internet access. Otherwise the transmitter re-registration procedure will require internet access.

For a sensor already started and running a session, a newly installed application on a different mobile phone or after any app data clear, does not know which transmitter to connect to, and whether that transmitter is already active. The application must connect to the transmitter to check for a "rejoinable" running session as it is the source of truth. A "rejoinable" session is any session where the transmitter is not in the failed / unknown / complete sensor states (stopped "ready" / in progress / interrupted "power cycled"), but the application will first verify the transmitter firmware version is supported and recall status (if possible). The backend must not be the source of truth for a running session - it is possible to start a session offline, and therefore possible a transmitter can be running without the backend's knowledge.

Primary connection flow: If the user still has their sensor packaging (or any other sensor packaging) to scan / manually enter the ID, they can follow the primary flow, however it is assumed that most users will dispose of the sensor packaging shortly after application - The secondary connection flow is required to reconcile with the requirement that a user attempting to start a session must be prompted to scan sensor packaging before physically applying it (in case it is recalled or expired), and for a new sensor this must also happen before connecting to it because the transmitter is not active until connected to a sensor.

Secondary connection flow: The application provides a "connect" button in the settings side menu, rather than the primary "guided" flow involving sensor packaging scanning. The connect button is shown either after manual disconnection (using the same button from the side menu, while in the connected state), or from a freshly installed application / application with cleared data. A user who changes phone or deletes the Bluetooth pairing mid-session, or finds that the pairing is no longer working (e.g. transmitter is disconnected and can no longer reconnect automatically or manually), can re-establish the BLE connection to the same transmitter, when there is an active session, without removing the sensor, and without removing the transmitter from the sensor. The connect button navigates to a "reconnect-only" version of the connection flow from the point of the Ble scanning UI onwards, which allows the user to select their nearby sensor, but with a flow that will only complete and remain connected if the sensor is already running a session (not failed / unknown / complete), essentially skipping the "scan sensor packaging" step. The user is not allowed to start a new session from this secondary connection flow, in which case they are redirected to the primary connection flow.

If the secondary connection flow connects but then detects the transmitter is not running a "rejoinable" session (failed / unknown / complete), it redirects the user to the start of the primary connection flow with an additional popup message guiding the user to apply a new sensor so they understand why their current one is not usable.

Note that users are able to start sessions offline and because of this after phone change or data deletion the app must have access to the sensor ID and session start time to be able to run the "start session" API call if the backend is not yet aware of the session. All information required to start the session in the backend must be persisted in the transmitter in case the backend hasn't been told of the running session (which prevents measurement upload until the session start API call). The primary connection flow inserts the sensor ID and session start time into the transmitter flash so it can be recalled again at any time during the running session and resolve this edge case.

If changing to a new phone, the user signs in to the same account, utilises the secondary connection flow, to select the Transmitter ID, and connects. Measurement history prior to the phone change is usually recovered from the server (previously synced data) but if not it will be recovered from the Transmitter via RACP for recent un-synced measurements (this consumes some additional sensor battery). The session continues with no sensor removal required. In this case to avoid user confusion, the primary flow has the option to directs the user to the settings page / secondary connection flow if they do not have the sensor packaging available, for when their session is already running.

If retaining the original phone and app, loss of a Bluetooth bond or other error condition directs the user to the CGM settings page and tells them to connect again through the secondary connection flow. The session should still be still active on the Transmitter and so re-pairing and re-authentication restores the connection.

Any measurements "missed" while the user is changing over to a new phone or restoring the connection will be stored on the transmitter as usual, ready to be sent across as soon as the procedure is complete. | 11: (iOS): No phone migration or session transfer flow exists. The application reconnects using a stored peripheral UUID local to the device. On a new phone, no mechanism retrieves the prior Transmitter identity from the server.

(Android): No phone migration flow exists. If a new phone connects to a Transmitter associated with a different user, USER_ID_MISMATCH is raised and the user is told to replace the Transmitter, rather than offering a recovery path. This is the opposite of the required behaviour.

(both platforms): No mechanism exists to retrieve the previously paired Transmitter identity from the server on a new device. The user must manually re-enter or re-scan the Transmitter ID.

DI-DO ROW 152 | 3: UN-124 Interruption Resilience | 4: DI-145 | 5: 727 | 6: 729 | 7: 846 | 8: The application must be able to recover from any "failed" API call where the original request reached the server and was processed successfully, but the application could not receive the response or required acknowledgement due to a network error part-way through the request. This is a potential condition where the application eventually makes the same request again, but the server already processed the request, and must only be considered successful after verifying the server holds the exact data/state intended. | 9: Idempotent API Re-Submission | 10: The scenario where the backend can potentially have data already saved that is different to locally saved data is extremely unlikely to happen as the user has to be either using multiple phones, actively clearing application data while offline, or encounter a transmitter interruption / resume at the same time as clearing application data.

When an API request for measurement upload reaches the server but the response is lost, the application later retries the same request (unless the local data has additional measurements or data which arrived in the meantime and the batch has enough space for the additional data). The server always returns stored data, and importantly when the server encounters and returns the "already stored" error, the data it has stored is returned. The application validates the correctness of its local data at this point, but never alters local data as it is considered a high risk to integrity if the server can drive all user applications to modify their existing data simultaneously (e.g. sytem error). For glucose data which is write-once and is not mutable, the application marks items which have failed the correctness check as "failed to upload permanently" and will not attempt retry of these items as they will fail again, and the app must move on to other upload batches otherwise other measurements will never get uploaded (the same batch would repeat indefinitely with failures). For non-glucose data where the API allows mutation the "failed permanently" state it not necessary and periodic retries will continue.

This applies to every API call where data is sent and persisted on the backend, including change of settings such as glucose thresholds.
DI-DO ROW 153 | 3: UN-124 Interruption Resilience | 4: DI-146 | 5: 728 | 6: 730 | 7: 831 | 8: The application must be resilient after an unintended CGM power cycle which can result in up to 9 previously delivered measurements becoming unavailable (not committed to flash), and potentially being delivered again if the session is resumed from an index already delivered (e.g. due to transmitter drift or incorrect local time). It must also be noted the application data could be cleared after readings were uploaded, so the same index attempts to upload again with a different glucose measurement. | 9: Power Cycle Session Recovery | 10: The transmitter resume session procedure takes a verified time and continues to run the session from that point. Any "skipped" measurements are marked as "invalid" in the transmitter flash, and note that in this scenario that up to 9 measurements marked as "invalid" could have previously delivered actual valid measurements to the app (or also have been invalid for a different reason). The app takes multiple steps to ensure it does not resume with a point that overlaps with already delivered measurements, to avoid receiving a second measurement with the same timestamp that differs:

After an unintended Transmitter power cycle (up to 9 flash-storage-uncommitted measurements potentially lost), the application retains the locally held measurements as long as the application data is not cleared. The locally held data is used to ensure when the interrupted transmitter session is resumed, that it resumes from a time/index after previously calculated measurements. Note that from this point onwards any measurements fetched through RACP will be "invalid", but the application can hold a valid measurement for those same indexes. In these cases it prioritises any (usually real and valid) measurement held and retains it for upload to the server. Note that resume time uses the trusted time cache to verify the local phone time and session resume can only deviate up to 3 minutes (3 measurements) from server time. Note that it is technically possible if the user is swapping between multiple phones with some internet outage that the "invalid" version of the measurement is uploaded to the server first, and if this happens then that becomes the source of truth, and the other application will continue to hold the valid measurement locally as long as the user remains logged in, but it will fail to upload.

If the application data is cleared, the login procedure will be followed again which reloads all the server held data (which if uploads suceeded was the same as the locally held data). If no locally held data is still available because the upload had failed for any reason, the transmitter session can be resumed as usual with trusted time verification, with any previously delivered measurements no longer held by the transmitter and app and backend being marked as "invalid", which happens during the resume session procedure.
DI-DO ROW 154 | 1: DI-310 | 2: APP-SRS-6.3.8 | 3: UN-124 Interruption Resilience | 4: DI-147 | 5: 310 | 6: 310 | 7: 832 | 8: The application must automatically reconnect after a CGM disconnection, within a reasonable period of time of the CGM becoming available again. | 9: BLE Auto-Reconnect | 10: After an unintentional BLE disconnection, while configured with an expected CGM session, the application automatically reconnects to the previously paired transmitter without manual user action.

It does this without explicit Ble scanning on both iOS and Android, with the operating system responsible for performing the connect in as timely manner as possible (gatt reconnect / retry = true). This is to prevent the system throttling calls to Ble scans, and to reconnect quickly after device deep sleep periods of Bluetooth disconnection.

Automatic Bluetooth gatt reconnection usually occurs within 60 seconds of the transmitter arriving in range of the mobile phone.
DI-DO ROW 155 | 3: UN-124 Interruption Resilience | 4: DI-148 | 5: 729 | 6: 731 | 7: 833 | 8: The application must recover from momentary Bluetooth transmission command failures, whether caused by the user, the phone, CGM range, or another dependency | 9: BLE Command Failure Recovery | 10: The application recovers from momentary BLE transmission command failures caused by range, phone state, or transient hardware errors.

If packets are received unexpectedly, or a command ack response is not given within 19 seconds, or a command data response is not given in 3 minutes, or a Bluetooth command error is encountered, the application initiates a force reconnect after 18 seconds. This can happen if the mobile operating system fails to register a disconnect quickly enough or caches packets and redelivers them after a rapid disconnect / reconnect cycle, or the transmitter is not notified of a rapid disconnect / reconnect and continues delivering responses the application is not expecting (e.g. RACP packet arrives when the application is not in the RACP receiving data state).

Once the application reconnects, recovery from the outage in a timely manner is ensured by first requesting the highest measurement index the transmitter has reached (with the "RACP Get Count" command), which is always requested after Bluetooth reconnection and session state checks (this applies to the in-progress and completed transmitter states), and then fetching the most appropriate range(s) of missing measurements immediately without delay. When selecting the next missing range to fetch, the application first prioritises any of the missing latest 15 measurements that relate to the real-time measurement display or the real-time trend arrow or the real-time alarming and alerts.
DI-DO ROW 156 | 3: UN-124 Interruption Resilience | 4: DI-149 | 5: 730 | 6: 732 | 7: 834 | 8: As soon as the application knows a measurement entry is missing, it must begin requesting all missing data from the CGM. This includes the connection restoration scenario after a sustained CGM disconnection. | 9: Missing Measurement Retrieval | 10: As soon as a measurement index gap is detected, the application requests all missing data from the Transmitter.

This applies during real-time measurement reception, an arriving index is compared against the last known persisted index for the session, and if there is a gap the RACP procedure to fetch missing measurements is utilised. A state machine ensures only one RACP range is requested at once.

This also applies after connection restoration without awaiting the next measurement, as each connection procedure executes the "get count" transmitter command (within in-progress or completed transmitter states), at which point any gap between the reported count and the known highest persisted measurement index can be known (otherwise only gaps between known persisted indexes can be surfaced until the receipt of the next real-time measurement). The application ensures it does not move straight into the normal real-time-only data receiving state before checking the transmitter count for an RACP that is required, so other application components can use the state reliably to deduce if there is any missing data (including while the transmitter is in the complete state) or to be more lenient when there is no missing data, and so the real-time-only data receiving state is not incorrectly entered when there is no more data to be received from inside the completed state.

Care is taken to ensure the get count command does not slow down the session start procedure, where it would report the first index as available before the application has received the first real-time measurement delivery, which would otherwise result in the application placing an unnecessary RACP request for that first measurement index.

Note that real-time measurements are permitted to arrive while RACP is running, and they are persisted as they arrive. Any ranges requested after new measurements are persisted will not request the data again as the next priority range selection is re-evaluated immediately before each range request until all missing ranges have had RACP procedures. Note that the transmitter may deliver a requested RACP index that then arrives via real-time and this is not an error condition, the first persistence is taken and never mutated.
DI-DO ROW 157 | 3: UN-124 Interruption Resilience | 4: DI-150 | 5: 731 | 6: 733 | 7: 835 | 8: After any unintended interruption to the application, the critical alarms (critical low glucose, critical disconnection) must continue to function. (e.g. application crashes and restarts, phone restarts, Bluetooth reconnection) | 9: Alarm Continuity After Interruption | 10: The critical low glucose alarm requires that the application remain alive (or have been restarted), and that the Bluetooth device remains actively connected, and transmitting, verified as matching the expected device / session, and receiving real-time measurements regularly. Critical low glucose alarm eligibility is derived from transient in-memory state of the latest real-time index, so that the latest real-time measurement can be guaranteed without any datetime comparison against untrusted local phone time and timezone issues, this is also the same requirement by the real-time trend arrow. Each measurement is persisted locally once received, along with an unsent flag. The measurement uploader has a state based design to batch and prevent network congestion if many uploads are necessary, and to correctly handle any start session API calls before sending measurements. DI-DO ROW 159 | 3: UN-124 Interruption Resilience | 4: DI-152 | 5: 732 | 6: 734 | 7: 845 | 8: Uploads which have failed to persist on the server must retry pediodically until successful, or the server is permanently rejecting the measurement (e.g. the read-only server data conflicts with locally held data). | 9: Upload Retry Until Server Confirmation | 10: Uploads that fail to persist on the server are retried periodically until the server confirms receipt or permanently rejects the record. The records are not marked as uploaded locally until the API call has succeeded explicitly.

The timing of the periodic retry depends on the type of failure, with additional randomised jitter applied on top of these timings to prevent server overload in case of server outage and all users failing at the same time (we do not want deterministic retry timing in this case):
* Server error rate limited error - Retry timing determined by the server and given in the response (e.g. 120 seconds)
* Server error with 0 previous fails - Retry after 15 seconds
* Server error with > 0 previous failures - Retry after 60 seconds
* Timeout / interrupted network with 0 previous fails - Retry after 1 second (start first retry soon as this failure probably took a while already and is likely to be a momentary interruption)
* Timeout / interrupted network with > 0 previous failures - Retry after 30 seconds
* DNS / Other network error - Retry after 30 seconds | 11: (Android)**: No background periodic retry (WorkManager or equivalent). Unsent records retry only on next measurement receipt or network status change.

DI-DO ROW 166 | 3: UN-125 Identify Real-time Data Issues | 4: DI-157 | 5: 737 | 6: 738 | 7: 850 | 8: The application must request confirmation of new sensor installation from the user, on any "interruption" of the CGM due to power cycling, in such a manner they understand the next steps to resolve the issue. | 9: New Sensor Confirmation on Session Interruption | 10: On a CGM session interruption (power cycling), the application asks through in-dashboard UI whether the user installed a new sensor or wants to continue the existing session. The user is guided to understand the question they are answering, as a power cycle could be from installing a new sensor early while the previous session was still running, or from a power-cycle failure (whether momentary or sustained) which does not mean the sensor is defective just that it is currently in an error condition and requiring attention from the user. They are informed that measurements will only be collected again after the confirmation is provided, and the no-data alarm will be continually reminding the user of the issue.

A state based solution detects the interrupted transmitter state, and displays the UI whenever the application holds an "expected session" for the user. The interrupted state is not cached to ensure correctness, and the options will remain available as long as the transmitter is connected, otherwise the usual disconnected state UI will take over until automatic reconnect and the transmitters interrupted state is fetched again.

If the interruped state is detected as part of the session start flow (the user does not have an "expected session" in progress), the user is asked for the same confirmation as part of the start session flow UI directly (not the dashboard UI), and if they inform that the existing session should be resumed the start flow's scanned sensor GS1 is discarded (as it may be different from the session to be resumed) and the previous session is resumed. Note that in this scenario the scanned sensor data could potentially not be available in the application if it had never been previously uploaded to the backend, though this is very rare as the user would have been repeatedly reminded by the "offline data" notification every 24 hours, to take care of this condition the application stores the sensor ID into the transmitter at the moment of session start, and it is always recalled (and confirmed to match the "expected session" before measurements are persisted) along with the other session info data (e.g. session start time).

When resuming a session, trusted time is required to be provided to the transmitter. This has the same correctness requirements as the trusted time that is calculated during the session start flow. The application attempts to call the backend API to fetch trusted time, and if it is not possible attempts to use the trusted time cache, and if that is not possible it asks the user to confirm their phone time and timezone is correct before proceeding. This UI is displayed after the user selects the option to resume the session.
DI-DO ROW 167 | 3: UN-125 Identify Real-time Data Issues | 4: DI-158 | 5: 738 | 6: 739 | 7: 851 | 8: The application must have functionality to display the BLE connection status. | 9: BLE Connection Status Display | 10: The application displays the current BLE connection status on the dashboard.

The primary states are as follows:

1) Connected, and session started and session fully verified (blue) - User intervention is not required, the transmitter is connected and is running the correct session and is in the non-terminal "in progress" state. Measurements are expected to arrive, and if they do not the no-data alarm will notify the user.

2) Temporary error (yellow) - User intervention is unlikely to be required, but the application is not currently receiving measurements. It expects the issue to resolve as soon as conditions allow:
  * The session start flow is proceeding (either connecting or connected) and it is not blocked awaiting user input, a new session is expected to start momentarily.
  * Disconnected and awaiting automatic reconnection when in-range (expected as long as pairing information is still valid. If pairing information is not valid the application is usually informed on loss, but it is possible this state is "endless" in certain error scenarios, the no-data alarm will continue to alert the user something is wrong.
  * Connected and reconnection startup sequence in progress and awaiting session info commands and verification.
  * Interrupted session resume in progress from the interrupted state, measurements will be available once it completes and start up is expected imminently.
  * A new AES key is currently being negotiated with the transmitter and backend. A new AES key is required due to either cleared app data or an encryption error with the transmitter. The application may be awaiting internet access, with a retry scheduled periodically.
  * A Bluetooth command error or erroneous packet was encountered, which necessitates an automatic disconnect and reconnect cycle, which will occur after 18 seconds.
  * The session has finished and the transmitter is now unexpectedly running a different session, the session info failed to match (transmitter in progress state, new session potentially started from a different mobile device). The application will finish marking the previous session metadata as finished with "unknown" cause, and will automatically move to assign the "expected session" to be aligned with this new information, so the user can continue receiving measurements from their new session automatically. This is only expected to happen in a very rare case where phones are swapped multiple times.

3) Error (red) - User intervention is required, the application is not going to be able to utilise the CGM without it. The user is also informed whether the transmitter is connected or disconnected while in this state as sub-state detail. Note that most terminal states disconnect the transmitter immediately to prevent self-denial-of-service (allowing phone change) but retain the reason in a "sticky" manner, in the application singleton. The following non-exhaustive conditions necessitate this status:
  * The application is attempting to start a new session, but it is blocked awaiting user input of time verification.
  * The transmitter is in the interrupted state, and is awaiting user input (either time verification or abort / resume choice).
  * The session has finished through completion, and is awaiting replacement of the sensor with a new one (transmitter completed state).
  * The session has finished through a failure condition, and is awaiting replacement of the sensor with a new one (transmitter failed or unknown state).
  * The session has finished through completion and a new sensor has already been installed and the application automatically reconnected to the transmitter (transmitter stopped state). The user must utilise the start session flow to provide sensor traceability before the session can be started.
  * Interrupted session abort in progress from the interrupted state, so it is known to be shutting down imminently.
  * Permissions are not granted or the Bluetooth toggle is not enabled such that connection would not be possible.
  * The phone OS-stored Bluetooth pairing is known to have been lost and the transmitter must be re-scanned and re-paired through the CGM settings menu or the start session flow (the transmitter will have a new MAC address which requires scanning of nearby publicly advertising BLE transmitters).
  * Other unexpected error - Bluetooth is reported as not supported on the given mobile phone (adapter not available), or the reported transmitter firmware is not supported.
DI-DO ROW 168 | 3: UN-125 Identify Real-time Data Issues | 4: DI-159 | 5: 739 | 6: 740 | 7: 852 | 8: The application must convey to the user when there is a problem which is expected to resolve itself over time. | 9: Auto-Resolving Problem Indication | 10: DI-739 defines temporary errors (yellow), which are conveyed to the user without individual detail of the technical scenario as automatic resolution is expected. DI-DO ROW 171 | 3: UN-125 Identify Real-time Data Issues | 4: DI-161 | 5: 741 | 6: 742 | 7: 854 | 8: The real-time trend arrow must not be displayed if the information it is derived from is not entirely complete, or becomes incomplete through a change in time resulting in outdated measurements, noting that phone time is also an untrusted user input and must not be used to determine this. | 9: Trend Arrow Suppression on Incomplete Data | 10: The real-time trend arrow is calculated in memory at display time from recent valid glucose measurements and is not persisted on disk independently of individual measurement persistence. Any readings with no valid glucose measurement - either those reported as unknown by the transmitter or not passing in-app sanity checks or entirely missing from the transmitter - result in the trend marker not being displayed. The trend classifier requires a complete 15-minute window ending at the newest valid real-time measurement index, with all 15 valid one-minute samples present in that window, to calculate average rate of change in mg/dL per minute across each pair of neighboring readings within the window. If the window is not entirely complete with all 15 present and fully valid measurements then the calculation cannot be made accurately and the trend marker is not displayed.

It is important the trend marker is not displayed when the last measurements are not available as this is a substantial part of indication to the user that the displayed glucose value is no longer realtime, and this is also the case when the transmitter is disconnected (and the user is then expected to check the date of the displayed measurement).

To avoid reliance on untrusted phone time and reliably function offline, the trend arrow does not utilise measurement timestamps or phone time at all. The "latest" real-time measurement index is maintained in memory by the real-time latest index module specified by DO-849, and watched for any changes

When the trend arrow is not displayed or calculated (for any reason), this means that the notifications which are directly launched from these calculations cannot function correctly. The no-data alarm is linked into the trend arrow calculation component so that it can respond accordingly and correctly with no missing overlap in coverage. Note that the no-data alarm begins as a medium-priority notification with escalation to critical priority, however the trend arrow notifications are at most medium-priority notifications and so do not need to trigger the full critical level of the no-data alarm. The no-data alarm tracks trend state separate from real-time availability state, and notifies the user with a medium-priority notification that the trend data is not available (an unknown trend may be rising or falling at the highest rate, so medium priority is appropriate).
DI-DO ROW 172 | 3: UN-125 Identify Real-time Data Issues | 4: DI-162 | 5: 742 | 6: 743 | 7: 855 | 8: "Critical" notifications (e.g. those impacting real-time measurements) must repeat periodically. | 9: Critical Notification Repeat | 10: Critical real-time alarm notifications remain active beyond the initial alarm delivery so the user continues to be alerted while the same alarm episode is still active. When a critical alarm is triggered, the application starts the in-app alarm UI and the operating-system notification dispatch together so in-app and system delivery stay aligned. The initial alarm episode schedules an immediate critical notification, then schedules a repeating notification request for the same event using a 60-second timer (which is the minimum repeat interval supported by the iOS notification framework). The repeating notification uses the critical alarm sound, carries the high priority alarm category / notification grouping, and sets flags where supported by the operating system so the alert continues to announce over the lock screen or over other in-use applications from the background. When the alarm condition or removed or the alarm snoozed, the application removes any pending and delivered repeat notifications for that event so the alarm does not continue to re-fire after acknowledgement, until the next alarm instance is necessitated.

The 60 second repeating timer is implemented through elapsed monotonic clock realtime (rather than UTC clocks) and retained in memory for reliability. If the application restarts, it immediately re-launches the critical alarm if the persistence source of truth states that the alarm has not been snoozed yet, and the 60 second periodic timer will restart in memory from that point.

DI-DO ROW 176 | 3: UN-126 Real-time Measurements | 4: DI-166 | 5: 744 | 6: 744 | 7: 859 | 8: The application must first prioritise the fetch of missing CGM readings which are required for calculation of the real-time trend arrow and real-time glucose display and critical low glucose alarm, over other missing readings (which may take much longer to fetch). | 9: Missing Measurement Fetch Prioritisation | 10: Note that the calculation of RACP ranges does not need to utilise the in-memory "latest" real-time index metric as specified in DI-742, the application uses a defined constant of 15 measurements for the trend arrow window to align the two behaviours and still achieve ideal component separation.

When the application evaluates the next missing range for the RACP procedure, if there is any missing measurement in the last 15 indexes (the exact same "window" that the real-time trend arrow calculation uses), the application prioritises these RACP ranges first, starting with the newest missing range (because as the data arrives this will continue to be relevant to the next trend).

Note that the trend arrow data is at most 15 measurements, so the RACP batch size can deliver all these items (if necessary) in a single packet.

The RACP windows must be checked regularly enough to ensure the application does not begin a fetch of an old and potentially very large range, which would then have to wait for completion before a small latest-15 (or less) range request could be requested (the RACP procedure requests one range at a time and then waits for all packets in that range to arrive before another RACP range is requested). To solve this issue the application never requests an RACP range greater than 495 measurements (it is divisible by 15 for transmission efficiency), which allows the next missing range calculation to re-evaluate relatively quickly.

DI-DO ROW 179 | 3: UN-126 Real-time Measurements | 4: DI-169 | 5: 747 | 6: 747 | 7: 861 | 8: The application must be able to collect CGM measurements at a rate equal to or faster than it "builds up", while the mobile phone is in a deep sleep/doze mode of operation. (e.g. Android device in deep sleep allows Bluetooth reconnects every 15-30 minutes, at which point the application must rapidly reconnect and pull all missed measurements before the next deep sleep cycle initiates, otherwise it will "fall behind") | 9: Continuous BLE Connection Maintenance | 10: Both platforms attempt to maintain BLE measurement collection in background, sleep, and (Android) Doze mode.

iOS: Background modes bluetooth-central processing are declared to attempt continual connection and never fall behind on minutely measurement packets with CoreBluetooth delivering characteristic notifications while the application is in the background. A background task scheduler provides periodic reconnection at a 5 minute minimum interval if necessary, and the connection procedure initiates RACP after a small number of session info commands which run on each reconnection. RACP pulls any missing measurements from the transmitter and the application is intended to stay alive for long enough to do so

Android: The operating system sleeps the application Bluetooth connection but not the application process itself, for periods depending on the level of sleep and manufacturer / model specific behaviour. The application holds a wake lock after each Bluetooth reconnection for long enough to fetch 3 full packets (3 x 15 measurements) of RACP data, which is long enough to fully fetch missing data from a 45 minute disconnection (the maximum expected through deep sleep). The wake lock times out after 58 seconds if this has not succeeded to prevent operating system throttling due to total wake lock duration over each 24 hour period - shorter wake locks are expected to shorten the deep sleep disconnection period. This RACP wake lock is considered a backup to the job scheduler 15 minute wake lock, which can be longer as it does not count toward system throttling limits. While the apps 15-minute keep-alive JobScheduler is running, the system holds an additional wakelock on behalf of the app, where the job reports completion after a simple in-memory 15 minute timer. Android versions <= 11 run a job for a maximum of 10 minutes before killing the job. Android versions > 11 may run jobs longer than 10 minutes if the system does not consider itself too busy (this is not well defined). RACP prioritises the real-time window for fetch, which will always begin requesting one packet with the latest (up-to) 15 measurements, ensuring that it should never fall behind with respect to the glucose alarms and notifications and trend arrow notifications even if the wake lock does not succeed for some reason.
* No sleep - Older Android phones (e.g. Samsung A13) often do not deep sleep.
* Light sleep - Before deep sleep is activated the OS usually enters a period of lighter sleep where the operating holds shorter disconnections of approximately 3-5 minutes. In between these disconnections it allows the application to remain connected as long as a wake lock is held, after which it will disconnect again.
* Deep sleep - After approximately 2 hours of light sleep the application enters deep sleep where the operating system holds disconnections of approximately 15-35 minutes (with a 15-minute keep-alive JobScheduler). In between these disconnections it allows the application to remain connected as long as a wake lock is held, after which it will disconnect again.

DI-DO ROW 181 | 3: UN-126 Real-time Measurements | 4: DI-171 | 5: 749 | 6: 749 | 7: 838 | 8: The real-time trend arrow must be displayed so the user can clearly tell if glucose is rising or falling at a medically relevant rate. | 9: Rate-of-Change Classification | 10: Both platforms classify the glucose rate of change into seven states using Transmitter-derived timestamps, not the phone clock. All 15 measurements within the trend window are required to be valid; if fewer are available, the trend state is none and no arrow is shown so the application does not display a direction unsupported by the available data. As time progresses new measurements must arrive to fulfil the all-15 requirement, otherwise the trend arrow disappears.

Measurements are also explicitly ordered by index to mitigate any accidental data ordering assumptions in the algorithm (measurement indexes are usually persisted in order but this is not always the case where RACP is used).

The average rate of change across each pair of measurements in the window (in mg/dL per minute) determines the real-time trend state. All measurements are already stored in mg/dL so no conversion is required.
- a rate above +3.0 is rapidly rising, 
- above +2.0 is rising, 
- above +1.0 is slowly rising, 
- between +1.0 and -1.0 (inclusive) is steady, 
- below -1.0 is slowly falling, 
- below -2.0 is falling, 
- below -3.0 is rapidly falling

The critical low glucose alarm utilises the same latest measurement real-time index source of truth as the trend arrow calculation and the no-data alarm as specified in DO-849 for 1:1 continuity.

When the value is at or below the threshold and no snooze is active for the critical low alarm, a critical low glucose alarm is raised immediately. The threshold check runs on every measurement, it is not batched or deferred. In the worst case of connectivity loss while bordering the critical threshold, the application could be launching both the critical low glucose alarm and the no-data alarm once per minute, but this design ensures safety and continual critical alarming until the user responds to (snoozes) both the critical low glucose alarms and critical no-data alarms. The alarm glucose comparison is made in mg/dL without any undue conversion, with the triggering unit displayed on the alarm screen in the user's display unit.

Measurements are processed for the alarms from the measurement source of truth which is the database, and are available immediately once packets have been processed and persisted. The real-time source of truth index in DO-849 updates immediately after persistence, so the critical low glucose component can always fetch this index from the database when it observes an update to the real-time index. The transmitter is always expected to be pushing the latest real-time measurement each minute while connected and in-progress, even while an RACP request is delivering batched missing measurements. Note that if the application just reconnected via Bluetooth it will need to wait for the next actual real-time measurement which is expected between 0-59 seconds later, however in this case the no-data alarm will have been handling the outage.

User-configurable low and high thresholds are separate controls and do not affect the critical low threshold.

Buckets with no measurements display no value, no zero fill or interpolated value is shown. Buckets which are missing too many data points from the most recent end of the timeline, with time compared to the latest measurement timestamp in the data utilised in the average chart (no dependence on untrusted phone time), will not display any average, to prevent the user accidentally utilising outdated average information. Too many missing recent data points is determined by taking the full timestamp range from all data utilised in the average chart (oldest to newest), determining the mid point of this time period, and counting items which fall before or after the mid point per-hour-bucket, and per-hour-bucket if there are at 2x or more items in the oldest range than the newest range the average is determined to be too out of date for that hour.

DI-DO ROW 237 | 1: DI-287 | 2: APP-SRS 6.1.1 | 3: UN-135 User Account & GDPR | 4: DI-229 | 5: 287 | 6: 287 | 7: 804 | 8: The application must allow new account registration. | 9: Account Registration Form | 10: The application exposes a Create Account entry point while the app is in an unauthenticated state. Selecting Register does not create the account through a native in-app form but the application launches the GlucoRx Keycloak web-hosted registration page using OpenID Connect Authorization Codethrough the phine's default browser. The hosted Keycloak registration form owns collection and validation of the account-creation fields, including the user’s email address, password, and other identity fields configured in the Keycloak realm.

Before opening the hosted registration page, the application stores only the temporary state needed to complete the verification round trip later, including the code verifier and registration redirect URI. When the user submits the hosted registration form successfully, Keycloak creates the account in a pre-verification state and sends the verification email. At this stage, the application does not create an authenticated session, does not exchange an authorization code for tokens, does not save an access token or refresh token, does not fetch profile data, and does not store date of birth, diabetes type, or other post-registration profile fields. The application returns the user to the registration-complete / verify-email state and allows a verification email resend request if needed. Email verification and later sign-in are handled as separate flows after account creation.

The application ensures an accidental back press does not delete registration entered data without user confirmation, and ensures registration form values are not cached while away from the registration form to resolve residual data privacy concerns.

Registration cannot proceed until the checkbox is activated and the form validation rejects submission if consent is not given.

The URLs for Privacy Policy and Terms & Conditions are defined as application-level string constants pointing to web-hosted documents, and the documents / URLs are common to all regions with any region-specific terms mentioned explicitly.
DI-DO ROW 239 | 1: DI-287 | 2: APP-SRS 6.1.1 | 3: UN-135 User Account & GDPR | 4: DI-231 | 5: 786 | 6: 786 | 7: 806 | 8: The application must allow login using email and password, for existing user accounts. | 9: Login and Session Bootstrap | 10: From the logged-out authentication entry point, selecting Sign In starts the Keycloak hosted sign-in flow for existing accounts. The user’s email address and password are entered on the Keycloak login page through a web browser session linked to the application using the user's default web browser on the mobile phone, not posted through an in-app native login API. The application launches the Keycloak OpenID Connect Authorization Code flow through the Keycloak authorization endpoint, and only processes the configured callback redirects. This keeps credential entry and related security concerns inside the system authentication browser session and outside the application UI layer.

When Keycloak accepts the credentials, it returns an authorization code through the configured redirect callback. The application exchanges that code for an access token and refresh token, then stores the returned tokens with the user ID. After token persistence, the application calls the profile endpoint with the new bearer token, saves the returned user profile as the signed-in user record, without local storage of any user password because Keycloak owns the credentials.

Following login, the application starts the Keycloak token keep-alive loop so the bearer is silently refreshed any time the refresh token is reported by the backend to be expired with a specific response error code (to avoid expiry time comparison with potentially untrusted local phone time).

If the browser sign-in is cancelled, the authorization code is missing, token exchange fails, or profile retrieval fails, the application remains in the logged-out state and does not keep a partial authenticated session. | 11: (Android): User credentials (email and password) are stored in DataStore for biometric re-authentication rather than in Android Keystore-backed encrypted storage.

DI-DO ROW 241 | 1: DI-364 | 2: APP-SRS-6.4.21.1 | 3: UN-135 User Account & GDPR | 4: DI-233 | 5: 364 | 6: 364 | 7: 808 | 8: The user must have the ability to log out of their authenticated user account, with awareness of the impact this will have on the CGM connection and data collection, with user application data retained locally for subsequent login (and upload if previously operating offline). | 9: Logout | 10: The logout option is not intended to be used regularly because it has important implications regarding CGM and remote monitoring alarms. The authenticated application exposes a Logout action from the Settings page under Account Security. Selecting this action presents a confirmation alert before any account state is changed. The confirmation message is session-aware:
*If no active CGM session exists it informs the user they will need to sign in again to view their health data, and that any pending data uploads will be paused.
* If a local or remote monitoring sensor session is still running it additionally warns that logout will prevent alarm functionality of both local CGM and any remotely monitored CGM, and that local CGMs will be disconnected requiring reconnection after the next login, and that any pending data uploads will be paused. 

When logout is confirmed, an API call is required to successfully perform the logout. The app notifies the backend which invalidates the tokens. If the API call is unsuccessful with an error code which is likely to be permanent, the logout flow continues anyway. If the API call is unsuccessful with an error code that is likely to be temporary, the logout does not proceed and the user is informed of the issue. Once the API call has been made successfully, the app executes the sign-out path which deletes locally stored authentication tokens and transmitter registration AES keys and retains the device-specific push notification registration and device-specific analytics and crash monitoring and retains all other user data and expected session data on the mobile phone, in an encrypted form for subsequent login (noting that the user can clear this data through application settings if required for security purposes). Retained data is always linked to a backend driven user ID, so that multiple sets of user data can be persisted without error. Other user data includes the expected CGM session so that CGM session can automatically reconnect and enable alarms with a previously in-use transmitter after re-login (and it will automatically follow the registration challenge flow to derive a new AES key as this was cleared on logout). Logout will disconnect any active transmitter connection and gRPC streaming connection for user data events and forget about any in-flight API calls relating to the logged out user and remove ongoing notifications sent to the system where possible and clear any in-memory caches held that are specific to the logged in user. The user is then directed to the sign-in flow.

DI-DO ROW 305 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 6: 815 | 7: 951 | 8: The no-data/disconnection alarms (all priority levels) must be resilient against incorrect untrusted user phone time, and resilience should continue while offline where possible. | 10: The no-data/disconnection alarms (all priority levels) are resilient against incorrect untrusted user phone time, and continues while offline, because it is based on realtime measurement arrival and a monotonic device clock to track invalidation of the last realtime measurement after 90 seconds. When a realtime measurement arrives, this is distinguished from an RACP historic/missing measurement fetch, it is marked as the latest, and utilised to feed into all alarms in the application, through the latest realtime measurement index component specified in DO-849. This does not utilise the measurement time at all and the component simply retains the latest measurement, along with an in-app monotonic clock timer to invalidate the measurement if 90 seconds passes without another arriving. From there either there is a measurement available and alarms are functional, or there is not a measurement available and the no-data alarm is functional instead, with no continuity gap.

Note that the trend alarms require additional measurements "behind" the latest realtime measurement, and a no-data alarm covers the condition where the realtime measurement is available but these other measurements are unknown, trend alarming and the additional no-data alarm are driven from the latest realtime measurement + the measurements immediately behind it.
DI-DO ROW 306 | 3: UN-124 Interruption Resilience | 6: 811 | 7: 923 | 8: On Android, if the mobile phone has restarted and not progressed further than the initial lock screen due to full disk encryption, direct boot hooks must be utilised to surface a no-data/disconnection alarm after an appropriate period of time. | 10: DO-706 specifies that a direct boot no-data alarm notifies the user if the application did not fully restart due to the phone not fully restarting.

On iOS it is not possible to mitigate this scenario.

On Android, the application detects if the mobile phone has not progressed past direct boot quickly enough, measured by a 3 minute timer (the same period of time utilised by the missing data watchdog). It does this using the direct boot hooks and stopping the timer once the full boot hooks are made. Note that the application database will not be available in direct boot as it is designed to be kept protected by the full device encryption, so the direct boot no-data alarm is always active regardless of logged in user, and does not require the database at all, for this reason it is a fully segregated stand-alone component from the rest of the application.

The no-data direct-boot alarm is designed to match a critical level alarm and can only be snoozed for 3 minute intervals to allow the user a moment to unlock the phone, and it continues until the user unlocks the phone for the first time (which will start up the full application). The snooze is timed in memory only and not permitted on disk.

Keep-alive measures that are specific to an active "expected session" are released after explicit user confirmation of the end of a session when the "expected session" data is cleared, after which the real-time alarms and components are not necessary (explicit user confirmation is defined in DI-834). The keep-alive measures which are dynamic and activate / release based on "expected session" to allow for updates are as follows:
* iOS / Android - Silent backend push notifications (does not block updates)
* iOS - Noisy visible backend push notifications (does not block updates)
* Android - Foreground "connected device" service
DI-DO ROW 309 | 3: UN-125 Identify Real-time Data Issues | 6: 834 | 7: 926 | 8: Application keep-alive persistence measures (e.g. Android foreground service) must remain active until explicit user confirmation of a finished session (after 15 days, failure state, etc.), because terminating persistence measures immediately at the end of a session risks the user not being notified that real-time measurements and alarms are no longer available until a new sensor is installed. | 10: The keep-alive persistence measurements related to an "expected session" always continue until explicit user confirmation of a finished or otherwise ended session. The "expected session" persisted app data is not cleared until this explicit user confirmation. This is crucial for the application to remain alive in the same persistent way as usual to notify the user continually while they do not know that measurements have ceased. The application never clears the "expected session" data from the database automatically, only ever from the explicit user button press defined below:

The user confirms a finished or otherwise ended session explicitly through the dashboard UI, with a button press alongside the terminal messaging (session finish can occur for a number of reasons) which always asks them to confirm they understand the sensor is no longer generating measurements, and they are also told that the button will stop collection of data and alarms for their CGM. Only after this button is pressed are they shown the guidance to replace their sensor. If the CGM is still fetching measurements from RACP during the terminal state (i.e. completed sensor), the UI to end the session is not displayed until this is complete (and in this scenario the application has no choice but to sound the no-data alarm (the user can snooze the no-data alarm) until it is fully complete). Note that old measurements are not expected to be fetching for any substantial period of time while the CGM is in the completed state.

In the unlikely case the application is still fetching historical measurements via RACP after the sensor terminates, it will continue doing so, and the user won't have the option to confirm session end (the button will be / appear disabled) until this is complete - Messaging will inform the user their session has ended but that they need to wait for measurements to sync from the transmitter before installing a new sensor. In this scenario the no-data alarm will continue to function to alert the user to the lack of real-time data and alarming, and the user will have to snooze it (repeatedly if necessary) until the historical data fetch is complete.

A finished or otherwise ended session is tracked by the presence of a number of terminal CGM states, retained in memory. If the application is terminated, it will reconnect to the CGM and determine the same state-based terminal state. The application disconnects once it sees this state (to allow the user to connect with a different mobile phone subsequently), but retains the terminal state in memory.

DI-DO ROW 311 | 3: UN-98 Medical Device | 6: 870 | 7: 927 | 8: Alarms and notifications must be designed so that multiple alarms at the same time do not interfere with each other, and so that the user is notified of the highest priority alarm first, but also of the other alarms as well without missing them. This applies between alarm priority categories as well as between different alarms of the same priority level. | 10: Low and medium priority notifications cannot interfere with each other by design - Multiple are tracked and permitted simultaneously, and the user can receive multiple of these simultaneously, with periodic repeats of each medium priority notification tracked on a shared timer for simplicity (this does mean that in the case of multiple medium priority events some of the medium priority notifications will initially repeat more regularly than the 15 minutes specified, to initially align with the already running shared timer).

Critical priority alarms are designed so that multiple critical priority alarms at the same time have the following priority order:
* Critical low glucose alarm - this is always the highest priority critical alarm and will show above all others.
* Critical no-data alarm - this can overlap with the actual critical low glucose alarm if the critical low glucose alarm is continuing to show / sound due to no user interaction, and the no-data alarm then activates. It ensures no continuity gap with the critical low glucose alarm, and to ensure this both can be active at the same time and will need to be snoozed one after the other. If the no-data alarm is triggering at critical level due to a "last available measurement" that is past the critically low glucose threshold, the no-data alarm triggers itself, as well as a critical low glucose alarm if the low glucose alarm is not already sounding.
* Critical recall alarm - sounds at a lower priority than the other critical alarms.
* Critical no-data direct boot alarm - can never display at the same time as other alarms (and this is ensured by the primary application so that even if the system calls the direct boot hook while the main application is loaded and active, the direct boot alarm will never trigger), the direct boot alarm does not utilise the application database as it is not available at that time due to encryption.

Sheet1 ROW 1 | 1: DI ID | 2: DO ID | 3: Design Output
Sheet1 ROW 2 | 1: DI-264 | 2: DO-647 | 3: The official Apple App Store is supported and is a trusted channel for distributing patient-facing iOS builds, it is most likely an uninformed user will attempt to search this trusted app store first.

The product IFU and packaging contains references and links to the Google Play Store to prevent confusion with malicious applications.

The listing metadata (e.g. name, description, screenshots, keywords, and category (Medical)) is maintained in the platform app stores, not in the source code. 

For iOS - Since no enterprise profile, ad-hoc profile, or direct .ipa install is allowed, users on managed devices where App Store access is restricted cannot install the application.
For Android - Android Enterprise managed delivery or third party APK distribution is not used for the released software.
Sheet1 ROW 3 | 1: DI-265 | 2: DO-648 | 3: Continued availability of the application on the App Store and Play Store depends on GlucoRx Ltd maintaining active membership in the Apple Developer Program and the Google Play Developer Program, and on each release submission complying with the respective platform review guidelines at the time of submission.

Software architects and developers and design controls are familiar with the terms and understand what system API usage is and is not permitted.

Changes to App Store or Play Store policies that affect the application's listing, permissions, or distribution eligibility are monitored as part of post-market surveillance under SOP-0035.

No ToS compliance logic is embedded in the application source code. Compliance is a process obligation managed at the point of each release submission, not a software function.

GlucoRx ensures the email address registered with app store distribution is active and monitored for alerts which require immediate attention as well as deadlines for required changes to the app binary.
Sheet1 ROW 4 | 1: DI-267 | 2: DO-649 | 3: Primary version availability, update notifications, and update rollout are handled by the App Store and Play Store respectively. This primary update channel includes functionality for staged roll out. 

When considering the app store and play store behaviours, there are a number of users who disable automatic updates (configured for each application), whether purposefully or accidentally  or forgotten. In this case the users will not receive automatic updates to the application through the standard platform mechanism. The procedure for a user to once again receive application updates in this scenario (including critical updates), is supported by a separate GlucoRx first-party internal version check API.

Note that automatic updates may be enabled but updates still not automatically installed due to application persistence features placing the application in an alive state where the system or updater is unwilling to update it (e.g. foreground service on Android), and in these cases the GlucoRx first-party internal version check API is also utilised to notify the user.

Due to the design of App Store and Play Store distribution, and the desire to use their staged rollout features, it is not immediately possible for the application to know when any new version update is available, even if the latest version was retained or fetched in the GlucoRx backend, noting that app store "latest release" APIs do not report staged rollout percentages. To address this deficiency, there are 4 levels of update checks depending on recall and update severity:
1) Optional updates not marked as "encouraged" or "recalled" through the recall API - Primary update channel remains responsible, with best-effort checks where the platform supports it periodically and before session start (before guidance to apply sensor) - This is currently Android only, through the "Google App Update Library", and is limited to phones with installed and updated Google Play services and with active internet connectivity. If a staged rollout is utilised this library will report the update to the user once it becomes available. If there is an update available on Android that the user has not installed automatically, it will be surfaced through the in-app UI and a low priority notification. iOS does not have such available functionality to check if an update is available to a given phone (staged rollout or not).
2) Updates marked as "encouraged" through the recall API. Where app fixes or improvements are substantial, the backend is configured to report these versions so both the iOS and Android applications can detect the available update (even if not-yet rolled out through staged release), and displays in-app UI directing the user to the relevant page of the app store where the update can be installed. This will be shown regardless of whether the user has automatic updates enabled, and will also help a user who has unintentionally disabled it to reconfigure that update setting. It is expected that updates are only marked as encouraged after staged roll outs are complete, and after time for the update to automatically install where possible, otherwise users will be told of an update that is not yet available to them.
3) Updates marked as "recalled - forbid next session" through the recall API. If the application version receives such a recall notice the current session is allowed to complete, after which new sessions cannot be started without performing an update (checked before sensor installation guidance tells the user to apply the sensor, in case it should not be applied before app update). The user is told through in-app UI after the check before sensor installation guidance (without any notification, not necessary as a session is not running). Note that a recall can be configured before an update is available, and in such cases the behaviour is the same, the user is told they need to update the application to continue and directed to the relevant platform app store regardless of update availability. Session resume is still permitted.
4) Updates marked as "recalled - stop immediately" through the recall API. If the application version receives such a recall notice the current session is not allowed to continue, measurements are no longer persisted or utilised by the application, and UI displays to inform the user they must update their application immediately, and the application immediately disconnects from any running CGM sensor session due to a recall of the application. No application features can be used other than the no-data alarm: the application process remains alive so the "no-data" alarm continues to function in this case to notify the user. Note that a recall can be configured before an update is available, and in such cases the behaviour is the same, the user is told they need to update the application to continue and directed to the relevant platform app store regardless of update availability.

Recall API calls are performed initially on each application start and also updated any time a "recall API change event" is received from the backend, and Google Play In-App Update API calls are performed periodically, as well as before starting a new session. Internet connectivity is required for the recall API but not for the Google Play In-App Update API. Caching behaviour and maximum age gates (when starting as session) for the recall API is defined in another DO, and Google Play Services is responsible for any caching of the latest available app update. If the Google Play In-App Update API call fails due to network errors then it is ignored (this is only ever used for optional updates not marked as "encouraged" or "recalled"). If the Google Play In-App update API check has failed due to an issue with Google Play services, the user is prompted to resolve these periodically through functionality provided by the library.
Sheet1 ROW 5 | 1: DI-266 | 2: DO-650 | 3: For the initial application release, the supported OS version range is evaluated against publicly available platform distribution data (App Store analytics for iOS and the Android distribution dashboard for Android) for the target geographic regions. The evaluation confirms that consecutive supported OS versions covers 90% of the target device population in those markets, noting that the publicly available statistics are an approximation.

When there is a new major version Android or iOS release GlucoRx considers when it is appropriate to stop distribution for the oldest versions, in such a way that maintains the device coverage target, considering maintenance costs and unavailable API features of older OS versions. This is done with the understanding that users with the application already installed will continue to have that version installed, however updates any new installs will no longer be available to them through the primary distribution channel. The internal version recall API is used to apply a killswitch when the build becomes too outdated.

The results of version evaluation, including data source, date, OS versions assessed, coverage percentage, and any proposed changes to the minimum deployment target are recorded in the release record.

There are many differences between different OS software across different manufacturers and model ranges and versions, and we have considered the following and minimised differences as far as possible; Google Play Services availability (fallbacks always implemented), Notification behaviour and styling (per manufacturer OS customisation), permission behaviour differences, keep alive differences (task kill behaviour and auto start preconditions), window decor theming differences, Bluetooth stack differences.

Sheet1 ROW 39 | 1: DI-312 | 2: DO-683 | 3: The application partitions data and processing by feature domain so that defects in one workflow are contained within that workflow’s storage, business rules, and synchronization path.

Persistent data is separated into distinct entities for independently owned domains such as authentication/session state, user profile, device and sensor session records, glucose measurements, calibration records, alerts and notifications, sharing, reporting/export, and queued upload operations.

Frequently mutated operational data is kept separate from read-only or rarely changed reference/configuration data, and derived or presentation-specific data is stored separately from source clinical records so that reporting, export, or UI defects do not overwrite the underlying measurement history.

State based design is utilised for the majority of the design so that the state of the application is always available and can be checked and validated and asserted in all conditions and combinations of conditions, and so that coding errors don't result in missed or incorrectly processed temporary events.

Each feature is implemented behind its own boundary, with typed models and feature-specific validation, mapping, and persistence logic. Presentation layers call these feature interfaces rather than reading and writing unrelated tables or shared mutable structures directly. Cross-feature interaction occurs only through defined contracts, such as identifiers, normalized domain models, or event notifications, instead of by allowing one feature to manipulate another feature’s internal storage.

Background sync, migration, and cache refresh routines operate on their own owned data sets and write scopes, with transactions limited to the affected domain.

The application database is treated as the ultimate source of truth, with transactions to ensure consistency through any errors. Domain specific singletons are utilised where possible to prevent potential threading issues and duplication of data is avoided where possible (including additional copies of derived data).
Sheet1 ROW 40 | 1: DI-313 | 2: DO-684 | 3: Each functional domain is stored in its own dedicated entity or table. Read-only reference data (CGM measurement data received from the transmitter, and manual journal entries) are stored separately from regularly mutated data (notification records, user settings).

The persistence layer uses platform-native typed data access mechanisms to reduce maintenance cost and the risk of introducing inadvertent data errors, with field mapping, unit conversion, and validation being centralised in a reusable manner. On Android, Room data classes provide typed field access with compile-time verification.

Non-null constraints are applied at the schema level on both platforms for fields where null values would represent a data integrity failure and foreign keys are used with the appropriate cascade setting to ensure data consistency across multiple tables. Transactions are utilised to prevent concurrent modifications from resulting in data errors when multiple fields or tables are being updated simultaneously and to prevent inconsistency after power loss or crash.

In memory caches are preferred over disk caches to prevent long-lived cache errors.

Sheet1 ROW 49 | 1: DI-322 | 2: DO-692 | 3: All clinical timestamps are stored and transmitted in UTC (millis, or seconds, or ISO 8601 format), making persistence independent of the device's local timezone setting and any user manipulation of the system clock.

The application trusted time module is used to warn the user with specific UI when the trusted time module is available and a discrepancy (+- 180 seconds) is detected / their local phone device time/timezone appears to be incorrect on:
* Session start - preventing the start.
* inputting events - preventing the entry.
* phone time/timezone change - through medium priority notification timestamped with the trusted time.

Note:
* If a discrepancy continues to remain unresolved and alarms or notifications are generated, any timestamps used for these in the journal or persisted in the database must be directly from the trusted time.
* Calibration does not utilise timestamps but sends the blood glucose measurement immediately to the transmitter to be applied from the next measurement index (if stable / accepted by the transmitter), and the application also ensures the provided measurement is not too old (due to waiting on the calibration screen before submitting).

Session start times are stored as UTC epoch values, and validated at the moment of creation with trusted time modules, with one exception where the user needs to start a session offline and the trusted time module is unavailable for this reason, in which case the untrusted phone time must be used but the user is asked to manually confirm the time/timezone is correct before proceeding. The BLE command layer on both platforms uses the trusted session start time, not the current phone clock, when deriving measurement timestamps. Note the session start time is stored in the transmitter and cannot be changed for the duration of the session and is retrieved and confirmed against the locally held value of session start time (along with transmitter, session index, etc.), avoiding any possible persistence or sync issues, and providing for offline derivation.

The application validates timestamps to ensure user events are never created in the future or too far in the past according to the local phone time, and the user will see an error message preventing the event from being saved if the phone time/timezone is detected to be incorrect during this validation. In the case where events are being created offline and the trusted time module is unavailable for any reason the user's local phone time is trusted temporarily until event upload when it is validated for obvious inconsistency by the backend. If the backend rejects the event due to it being timestamped too far in the future, the event is removed from the local data store of the application and the user is notified with a medium priority notification.

Sheet1 ROW 64 | 1: DI-342 | 2: DO-706 | 3: Once a CGM session is active, the application remains operational in the background and restarts automatically after termination, without requiring user interaction. Multiple keep-alive methods are employed in combination to maximise reliability, because the mobile operating system aggressively optimises applications and is well known to terminate or suspend them.

On iOS, complementary keep-alive methods are configured considering the three states (active - fully in memory and executing code, suspended - fully in memory but not executing code, terminated - ):
1) Enabling "run in background support", with a scheduled background task for periodic application refresh, with a requested rate of 300 seconds, executed at approximately 15-30 minutes by the operating system. If being used to restore the application from the terminated state, it will only be able to keep the application alive for a shorter time, approximately 5 minutes (and periodically). This does not help with the suspended state.
2) Active Bluetooth low energy connection (or active reconnection request), with bluetooth-central background mode. This helps prevent the suspended state and keep the app in the active state.
3) CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey allows iOS to relaunch the app after it was terminated so Bluetooth activity can continue. This will trigger when coming back into Bluetooth range from a disconnected CGM.
4) "Silent" push notifications dispatched from the backend during a session (external to the application) prevent the application from remaining in the suspended state indefinitely.
5) "Noisy" push notifications dispatched from the backend during a session (external to the application) if the backend has not received session data for the last 30 minutes, to encourage the user to re-open the application from a terminated state when other mechanisms have failed (interactivity is required.

On Android, complementary keep-alive methods are configured considering the two states (active - fully in memory and executing code, terminated - no memory and no code execution):
1) Android foreground service with the connected-device service type and ongoing notification, helps the operating system understand the application is required for the ongoing CGM session and should not be terminated.
2) Companion device manager is utilised for the bluetooth pairing which creates an additional "association" with the operating system, which makes application death less likely and the application configures an OS-level service which registers to receive associated "device appeared" callbacks, which can bring the application back from a terminated state.
3) The user is guided to and must configure the application battery optimisation exemption request, mitigating certain application doze and standby restrictions.
4) Android job service registers the application for periodic pings at approximately a 15 minute period (the fastest available). This is able to persist after application death and restarts the application if necessary.
5) The application registers with the system for startup after phone reboot. On some mobile phones this requires an additional permission / user configuration, which the application aims to prompt as required (but note there is no official API for this, so it is a heuristic). If the boot receiver is not executed the other mechanisms would be used.
6) Push notifications dispatched from the backend (external to the application) bring the application back alive from a terminated state when other mechanisms have failed.
7) Direct boot no-data alarm notifies the user if the application did not fully restart due to the phone not fully restarting.
