Sheet1 ROW 70 | 1: DI-348 | 2: DO-712 | 3: Before the application persists any received measurements, sends any RACP requests, or issues any session modification commands, it verifies that the transmitter, firmware version and session are as expected. It is noted that the process of firmware update is only performed outside of a session because it is utilises the same flash where measurements are stored. (In development it is possible to update boards without this limitation so the code is written to handle and support it either way).

Delayed persistence until verification of transmitter serial (A), firmware version (A), expected active session identifier, expected active session start time:
After every bluetooth connection is initiated (and on each re-connection), the Modus state machine initialises from scratch. Measurements are not persisted until one of a number of data accepting states have been reached. Before these states have been reached, to save re-transmission via RACP later, a list of received measurement-specific data packets (encrypted and unparsed) are stored in memory as long as the correct transmitter remains connected until the application has completed the verification process, at which point it attempts to decrypt and persist them:
1) The state machine first executes the device info command and verifying the returned transmitter serial number matches the expected session persisted locally, and verifying the returned firmware version is within a range supported by the application. A mismatch moves to a terminal error state.
2) The state machine then executes the device status command and verifying the returned state is IN_PROGRESS to proceed towards the data accepting states. A mismatch moves one of the "session ended" terminal states.
3) The state machine then verifies the transmitter specific AES key is available, and if not, performs the key challenge procedure before proceeding.
4) The state machine then executes the in progress session info command and verifying the returned session index and returned session start time matches the expected session data persisted locally. A mismatch moves to the "session ended" terminal state. This command is also executed with the optional encrypted=true flag, which allows the app to get an immediate response indicating if the app's stored AES key is incorrect (rather than waiting for the next data packet decrypt operation or RACP request to fail).
5) The state machine then moves to one of the data accepting states (including a state which utilises RACP commands if necessary), and immediately processes any measurement packets which were buffered during the state machine initialisation flow before proceeding.

Delayed persistence until verification of transmitter serial (B):
* Before any modification commands or received health data can be utilised, the application must have the correct AES key to encrypt and decrypt command payloads for the Modus application-layer encryption (this is in addition to Bluetooth communication encryption). This is the first implicit step of transmitter verification, because the AES key persisted in the app is transmitter-unique and generated by the backend with a challenge process to guarantee the transmitter is genuine. The app negotiates this key before utilising the transmitter, or re-negotiates it if there is an error in decryption, and it is persisted locally against transmitter serial number thereby implicitly verifying it. Note that some simple commands such as device info and device status are not encrypted, but all health information has the encryption applied.

Delayed persistence until verification of firmware version (B):
* The application requires and checks for a specific UUID associated with the supported firmware version(s). Modus protocol is to update the UUID used by transmitter firmware on breaking API changes. If the firmware has been updated with breaking changes and the application is outdated, it simply will not communicate with the new firmware, so no transmitter commands will be executed, and no measurements will be received or persisted.

Sheet1 ROW 72 | 1: DI-365 | 2: DO-714 | 3: When the user stops the critical low glucose alarm, it is performed as a "snooze" function. This reliance on real-time measurements is to ensure safe-by-design behaviour that ensures this alarm is not based off of untrusted device time to determine the "freshness" of the last received measurement which may or may not be realtime any more. Incorrect device time could potentially be an issue when the trusted time cache is not available (e.g. offline usage after phone or application restart).

If the CGM has stopped delivering real-time readings, user communication of this is handled through the no-data alarm specified in other requirements.

If a new measurement arrives above the critical low threshold while the alarm is snoozed, the snooze period continues counting down (rather than resetting) to prevent nuisance alarms if the measurements are cycling above and below the threshold.

If the session ends with explicit user confirmation while the alarm is snoozed, then the snooze (and any active critical low alarm) is reset / cleared ready for the user's next session.

Sheet1 ROW 77 | 1: DI-375 | 2: DO-719 | 3: All CGM glucose timestamps are derived from the sensor session start time, which is stored in UTC, making them independent of the device's local timezone setting. To meet the requirement that sensor sessions must be startable while the user does not have internet connection, the apps attempt to maintain a long-lived trusted time cache  from the last successful API call, which can estimate a trusted server time from each device's internal monotonic clock, time since boot, this is available as long as the phone or application is not restarted. The trusted time modules are also utilised for interrupted session resume, which requires the current time to be sent to the transmitter.

Due to potential monotonic clock drift of the trusted time cache and the trusted server time including a network latency element, the server time is only used for the deviation check and the untrusted phone time is the actual utilised value when within acceptable tolerance (phone time is less likely to drift than our cache when correct).

If the trusted time cache is not available for session start or resume (e.g. offline usage after application restart), the user must still be able to start a new CGM sensor session, and is prompted to manually confirm the time and timezone is correct.

The snapshot used for time derivation attempts to update periodically every 60 minutes if internet is available, and also attempts to update during the new session flow (and the UI waits for this additional re-check). This periodic refresh and refresh during the new session flow is necessary as the monotonic clocks do drift with device deep sleep, lock screen activity and charging, so are only used to validate the user's untrusted phone time is within 180 seconds of the estimated server time.

1) Session start time is a critical parameter for the transmitter which must also use validated local phone time, and does so with the same trusted time snapshot module "cache" described here. Given that sensor expiry is validated at roughly the same time as the session start time is needing to validate the local phone time, the offline support for these two is strongly related and implemented in a shared manner.
2) The application attempts to notify the user if they are offline for the recall check API, and this should encourage them to resolve connectivity issues ahead of a potentially failed trusted time API call.

Note that for the following reasons the transmitter expiry date is not extracted from the GS1 barcode on transmitter packaging or the transmitter itself via an in-app camera feature, but fetched from the backend and based on the transmitter serial number which the CGM reports through the Bluetooth connection:
1) Sensor packaging is different from transmitter packaging, and due to the reusable nature of the transmitter, it is assumed the user will have discarded the transmitter packaging after first use.
2) Once the transmitter is attached to a sensor the barcode printed on the transmitter is face down and inaccessible.
2) Once the transmitter is attached to a sensor (required to start receiving power and connect), even if there was an outer barcode it would likely be physically out of reach on the back of an arm for the user in terms of barcode scanning with a camera.

Safe by design - The first time a transmitter is used in the application (or after app data clear), it must have an internet connection to negotiate the transmitter encryption keys with the backend. These keys are persisted and unique to each transmitter registration, and the application also fetches the transmitter expiry date from the backend, and persists it alongside the encryption key. When the encryption key is cleared due to app reinstall or data deletion, internet connection is required again to re-register for another encryption key, so the expiration date will always be available alongside the verified genuine transmitter encryption key without fail.
Sheet1 ROW 82 | 1: DI-311 | 2: DO-735 | 3: FIRMWARE CRITICAL UPDATES (AT SESSION START):
(Shared base recall/update fetch and persistence logic): The application polls the server on application startup and then opens a gRPC stream to receive real-time updates to the firmware recall notices / critical update version mappings (update mapping must be optional in case the recall needs to be made before firmware update is available). The stream reconnects as soon as network becomes available with gRPC streaming behaviour. The recall notices are persisted with a timestamp of when they were last fetched / checked, and if the timestamp is outdated by more than 24 hours it indicates the server has been unable to be contacted to fetch the recall notices (measured against trusted time cache  or local phone time if unavailable), the user is notified that the application has been unable to connect to the internet to upload measurements and ensure safe usage, with a low priority notification that re-triggers every 24 hours until the recall notices are refreshed. Recall notices are persisted locally for offline usage.

There is no blocking functionality based on the age of the recall cache for offline usage, however the application attempts to call the recall API to refresh the persisted recall notices at the moment it is needed during the session start flow (in additional to the other checks), awaiting the result but proceeding regardless of refresh outcome for offline usage.

The current transmitter firmware version is retrieved on each connection to the transmitter through BLE, including immediately before a new CGM session begins, if a recall is affecting the installed firmware, the user is shown non-blocking UI to inform an update is necessary (note this is based on recall status not update availability), and the application calls a backend API to receive the best update binary (if available) while preventing the user from proceeding with the session start if the call or the firmware download or firmware install cannot complete successfully.

If a mandatory firmware update is pending, the user is directed to the firmware update process, which is a dismissable firmware update screen, and download/install begins immediately without user intervention or confirmation. The firmware is downloaded and applied as long as the transmitter remains connected. Any failure to download prompts the user to retry. The user must always have the option to leave the download/install screen to prevent usage of historical glucose data and in case a system error is rendering the transmitter unusable and access to customer support information is required. If the transmitter disconnects the download continues until complete in the background (singleton implementation), even if the user exits (and the downloaded file persists in the application-secure directory to speed up the update process on the next connection). If the transmitter disconnects the user is returned to the BLE scanning/pairing screen with the usual error where they can retry the connection.

A state machine tracks progress through starting, uploading, and completed phases. On successful completion, after the new firmware version is re-checked and confirmed through the transmitter API, the blocking state is cleared and the session start flow is permitted.

Sheet1 ROW 104 | 1: DI-465 | 2: DO-746 | 3: The BLE protocol layer itself is utilised for encrypted communication and integrity checking.

In addition to the BLE layer, Modus application layer encryption and integrity checking is implemented when protected commands and PII is in question: On initial transmitter registration, the embedded Firmware generates a cryptographically random registration challenge and transmits it to the iOS/Android app. The app forwards this and the device serial number to the Backend API. The apps also ensure unique nonce usage for every command payload that is sent to the transmitter. The session key is persisted in the app as long as possible so that future sessions can be started with the same transmitter offline. The DRK never traverses the BLE channel or internet channel. The iOS/Android app does not possess the DRK and cannot derive the SessionKey independently. Any tampered packets are detected and discarded at the recipient's authentication tag verification step.

Sheet1 ROW 131 | 1: DI-718 | 2: DO-821 | 3: The no-data alarm is designed to operate from the same data source of truth (DO-849) as the critical low glucose alarm, to ensure full coverage across the combination of the no-data and the critical low glucose alarms (DO-835 / DO-864). Only the last expected measurement index impacts the no-data alarm as it relates to coverage for the critical low glucose alarm, fetching older measurements from RACP does not help the user if real-time measurements are missing. A triggered no-data alarm resets its snooze and sounding condition if the last expected measurement arrives again, unlike other critical alarms which continue until explicit user confirmation (noting that the last expected index continually increases as time elapses).

The no-data alarm is also designed to operate from the same data source of truth (DO-849) as the trend arrow calculation and the trend arrow rapidly falling / rising notifications, with additional behaviour relating to the measurements immediately before the latest index to ensure full coverage across the combination of the no-data alarm and the trend arrow notifications (notifications defined in DO-854). If the latest index is missing the no-data alarm will sound already to cover the loss of the critical low glucose alarm, the trend arrow calculation utilises the 14 measurements immeditely before the latest index (for a window with 15 measurements). The no-data alarm utilises the same constant that the trend component has to prevent accidental misalignment in future. The no-data alarm only ever raises a medium priority notification if any of the 14 rapidly falling or rising arrow related measurements are missing, as this the highest priority the rapidly falling / rapidly rising notifications are ever dispatched with.

There are multiple scenarios which prevent the critical low glucose alarm from functioning:
1) During remote monitoring measurements from another user - Internet connection is continually required.
2) Mobile phone hardware issues: Speaker / Amplifier malfunction, screen malfunction.
3) The uncontrolled nature of mobile phone operating systems and environments, where applications do not have the ability to fully control the phone or override certain user settings (Bluetooth enabled, Do not Disturb, notifications, lock screen security, speaker volume) because they run in a heavily sandboxed manner. This is further complicated by multiple versions of operating system as well as manufacturers customisation of the operating system environment so that there are a large variety of phone OS behaviours in circulation.
4) Reliance on the phone to continually maintain a Bluetooth connection: Mobile phone OS deep sleep periods sustaining periodic Bluetooth disconnects (usually while the phone is plugged in and charging). Note that the mobile phone updating or shutting down or restarting without the user unlocking after boot presents a scenario where the alarm or even notifications cannot function and the iOS application or CGM cannot react after-the-fact to this scenario, so the application attempts to warn the user of impending low phone battery in advance where possible.
5) Reliance on hardware to generate real-time measurements, which has a number of temporary or permanent interruption scenarios, sensor placement issues, physical sensor damage, physically applied pressure / torque, sensor chemistry lifetime, sensor battery issues. Permanent issues with the sensor are usually reported as failure states in the transmitter, but this is not assumed or guaranteed.
6) Reliance on real-time measurements continually arriving from the transmitter uninterrupted, including wireless connection interference, wireless range compromise, transmitter failure states, bluetooth disconnections.
7) Continual application permissions (note that the actual revoke action will terminate the application, but it should restart again afterwards), Bluetooth permission, 

DI-733 defines how the critical no-data alarm is resilient to application and phone restarts, including direct-boot-only partial phone restarts on Android.

The medium priority and escalated critical priority no-data alarm is used to cover any scenario where the critical low glucose alarm cannot function, other than entire phone shutdown which cannot be covered by any alarm - If the application is alive and has not received any recent measurement values (including measurement packets which arrived but without glucose values [this condition is suppressed until after warm-up], or glucose values which arrived but failed the application's sanity checks, or measurement packets which did not arrive at all for any reason) for the last 3 minutes / 3 measurement indexes (this time is purposely the same as the Bluetooth no-data state check after 3 minutes, as the usual outcome of this state check would be sensor failure), the no-data alarm is initiated.

The no-data alarm will begin as a medium priority alert and escalate to critical severity after a period of time, which is chosen initially based on how low the last glucose measurement was, and can be escalated immediately when the no-data is encountered at a relatively low glucose level. Escalation time is based on in-memory elapsed realtime as long as the application does not restart. If the application restarts the correct no-data escalation timer is restored with the correct remaining time, based on the trusted time module where possible, or untrusted phone time if not. This watchdog timer continues without erroneous reset even in a Bluetooth disconnecting and reconnecting cycle and/or remaining disconnected.

The medium priority no-data notification will pester the user every 15 minutes as long as the no-data issue remains unresolved. The critical no-data alarm is equivalent in volume and severity to the critical low glucose alarm. Critical no-data snooze is similar to the critical low glucose alarm, but tracked separately, permitting snooze up to 1 hour each time, with no upper limit on the number of snoozes. A snoozed no-data alarm cannot be reactivated early by direct user interaction through the settings like the critical low glucose alarm (to prevent confusion). Explicit user interaction is required with the same randomised location-press UI as the critical low glucose alarm. If the app is in the background, the UI will brought to the foreground when alarming in the exact same manner as the critical low glucose alarm.

The timing and glucose levels consider the following logic for designing against nuisance alarming:
* The patient usually begins sleep between 5-6 mmol/L, delay time until critical is considered as "time before waking an asleep user who did not notice the medium priority no-data alarm".
* The delay time is to allow the transmitter time to reconnect gracefully before sounding a critical alarm.
* The critical low glucose alarm threshold is fixed at 3.1 mmol/L.
* Android deep sleep disvonnects occur for approximately 15-35 minutes at a time, and so would inherently trigger the no-data alarm, escalation to critical priority during this period should be avoided if not necessary by utilising the last known glucose value to delay safely.
* A no-data scenario from a lower glucose value must escalate to critical sooner.
* A no-data scenario from a glucose value below 4.0 mmol/L must escalate immediately.
* A no-data scenario from a glucose value between 4.0 (inclusive) - 5.0 mmol/L (exclusive) must escalate after 0 - 22 minutes, determined linearly.
* A no-data scenario from a glucose value between 5.0 (inclusive) - 10.0 mmol/L (inclusive) must escalate after 37.5 - 90 minutes, determined linearly. This is a much longer delay than a scenario from glucose values below 5.0 mmol/L as it carries substantially less risk and so nuisance alarming can be prevented safely.
* A no-data scenario from a glucose value above 10.0 mmol/L must escalate after 90 minutes.

The system is designed to permit session initialisation offline as much as possible. The first-time transmitter registration must be performed online, after this offline ability is retained as long as the application database exists (the transmitter encryption key  is retained). The first-time CGM setup often immediately follows application download and user registration, and so internet access is expected. The sensor/transmitter session start procedure depends on the transmitter's current registration state which is held in the backend, and by extension the registration state held in the application:
* Transmitter not yet registered: The user must have internet access, and scan the GS1 barcode or manually enter the pairing PIN during the transmitter registration flow.
* Transmitter registered, app database holds empty or invalid key: The user must have internet access, no barcode scan is required.
* Transmitter registered, app database holds valid key: No internet access is required.

The system is designed to permit session initialisation offline as much as possible. Session start or resume usually depends on the availability of trusted time:
* Trusted time cache not available: No internet access is required, the user must confirm their local phone time is correct manually.
* Trusted time cache available: No internet access is required.

The sensor/transmitter session start procedure depends on the transmitter's current state which is fetched via Bluetooth after successful connection:
 * Session Stopped: Session start is initiated automatically. The application sends a StartSession command containing the trusted and verified start timestamp (seconds UTC), which was verified against server time or manually confirmed by the user. This trusted time is then persisted in the transmitter, and it is utilised to calculate trusted time values for each measurement based off measurement indexes (without utilising local user phone time, which can be incorrect). Session metadata is persisted locally on both platforms and reported to the backend.
 * Session In Progress, warming up / stabilising: A dedicated warmup progress screen is displayed, showing a progress indicator driven by estimated warmup remaining time. A warmup watchdog is in place: if the transmitter does not complete the warm up by the 3h mark (measured by transmitter index, essentially trusted time), the application will inform the user the sensor has failed and direct them to replace it. The measurement activity watchdog is armed: if the transmitter is connected but no new index is received within 3 minutes on an active session, the session status command is used to determine the actual state (in case the transmitter moves to failed or unknown states). RACP data recovery is performed for any missing indexes. The no-data alarm will not trigger based on lack of glucose values.
 * Session In Progress: The application navigates to the dashboard and begins receiving valid measurements. The measurement activity watchdog is armed: if the transmitter is connected but no new measurement is received within 3 minutes on an active session, the session status command is used to determine the actual state (in case the transmitter moves to failed or unknown states). RACP data recovery is performed for any missing measurements.
 * Session Completed: RACP data recovery is performed for any missing measurements, then the user is directed to replace their sensor. The power interruption of sensor replacement will transition the transmitter from the completed state to the stopped state (not the interrupted state).
 * Session Interrupted: This is usually caused by the user replacing their sensor early, without using the application UI to do so and cleanly shut down the previous session. The user is asked whether they have applied a new sensor or whether the application should continue with the existing sensor, and either aborts or resumes the existing session in response.
 * Session Failed / Unknown: Sensor replacement guidance is shown.

Sheet1 ROW 149 | 1: DI-732 | 2: DO-834 | 3: As soon as a measurement index gap is detected, the application requests all missing data from the Transmitter.

This applies during real-time measurement reception, an arriving index is compared against the last known persisted index for the session, and if there is a gap the RACP procedure to fetch missing measurements is utilised. A state machine ensures only one RACP range is requested at once.

This also applies after connection restoration without awaiting the next measurement, as each connection procedure executes the "get count" transmitter command (within in-progress or completed transmitter states), at which point any gap between the reported count and the known highest persisted measurement index can be known (otherwise only gaps between known persisted indexes can be surfaced until the receipt of the next real-time measurement). The application ensures it does not move straight into the normal real-time-only data receiving state before checking the transmitter count for an RACP that is required, so other application components can use the state reliably to deduce if there is any missing data (including while the transmitter is in the complete state) or to be more lenient when there is no missing data, and so the real-time-only data receiving state is not incorrectly entered when there is no more data to be received from inside the completed state.

Care is taken to ensure the get count command does not slow down the session start procedure, where it would report the first index as available before the application has received the first real-time measurement delivery, which would otherwise result in the application placing an unnecessary RACP request for that first measurement index.

Note that real-time measurements are permitted to arrive while RACP is running, and they are persisted as they arrive. Any ranges requested after new measurements are persisted will not request the data again as the next priority range selection is re-evaluated immediately before each range request until all missing ranges have had RACP procedures. Note that the transmitter may deliver a requested RACP index that then arrives via real-time and this is not an error condition, the first persistence is taken and never mutated.

Sheet1 ROW 152 | 1: DI-734 | 2: DO-845 | 3: Uploads that fail to persist on the server are retried periodically until the server confirms receipt or permanently rejects the record. The records are not marked as uploaded locally until the API call has succeeded explicitly.

The timing of the periodic retry depends on the type of failure, with additional randomised jitter applied on top of these timings to prevent server overload in case of server outage and all users failing at the same time (we do not want deterministic retry timing in this case):
* Server error rate limited error - Retry timing determined by the server and given in the response (e.g. 120 seconds)
* Server error with 0 previous fails - Retry after 15 seconds
* Server error with > 0 previous failures - Retry after 60 seconds
* Timeout / interrupted network with 0 previous fails - Retry after 1 second (start first retry soon as this failure probably took a while already and is likely to be a momentary interruption)
* Timeout / interrupted network with > 0 previous failures - Retry after 30 seconds
* DNS / Other network error - Retry after 30 seconds

  * Interrupted session abort in progress from the interrupted state, so it is known to be shutting down imminently.

  * Other unexpected error - Bluetooth is reported as not supported on the given mobile phone (adapter not available), or the reported transmitter firmware is not supported.

The RACP windows must be checked regularly enough to ensure the application does not begin a fetch of an old and potentially very large range, which would then have to wait for completion before a small latest-15 (or less) range request could be requested (the RACP procedure requests one range at a time and then waits for all packets in that range to arrive before another RACP range is requested). Sheet1 ROW 171 | 1: DI-747 | 2: DO-861 | 3: Both platforms attempt to maintain BLE measurement collection in background, sleep, and (Android) Doze mode.

Android: The operating system sleeps the application Bluetooth connection but not the application process itself, for periods depending on the level of sleep and manufacturer / model specific behaviour. The application holds a wake lock after each Bluetooth reconnection for long enough to fetch 3 full packets (3 x 15 measurements) of RACP data, which is long enough to fully fetch missing data from a 45 minute disconnection (the maximum expected through deep sleep). The wake lock times out after 58 seconds if this has not succeeded to prevent operating system throttling due to total wake lock duration over each 24 hour period - shorter wake locks are expected to shorten the deep sleep disconnection period. This RACP wake lock is considered a backup to the job scheduler 15 minute wake lock, which can be longer as it does not count toward system throttling limits. While the apps 15-minute keep-alive JobScheduler is running, the system holds an additional wakelock on behalf of the app, where the job reports completion after a simple in-memory 15 minute timer. Android versions <= 11 run a job for a maximum of 10 minutes before killing the job. Android versions > 11 may run jobs longer than 10 minutes if the system does not consider itself too busy (this is not well defined). RACP prioritises the real-time window for fetch, which will always begin requesting one packet with the latest (up-to) 15 measurements, ensuring that it should never fall behind with respect to the glucose alarms and notifications and trend arrow notifications even if the wake lock does not succeed for some reason.
* No sleep - Older Android phones (e.g. Samsung A13) often do not deep sleep.
* Light sleep - Before deep sleep is activated the OS usually enters a period of lighter sleep where the operating holds shorter disconnections of approximately 3-5 minutes. In between these disconnections it allows the application to remain connected as long as a wake lock is held, after which it will disconnect again.
* Deep sleep - After approximately 2 hours of light sleep the application enters deep sleep where the operating system holds disconnections of approximately 15-35 minutes (with a 15-minute keep-alive JobScheduler). In between these disconnections it allows the application to remain connected as long as a wake lock is held, after which it will disconnect again.

Sheet1 ROW 247 | 1: DI-810 | 2: DO-881 | 3: Note the no-data alarm covers safety / alarming of the missing data scenario in all cases including this transmitter cessation scenario, however this DI specifically refers to the application's ability to respond appropriately to the transmitter state changing unexpectedly (i.e. moving to the failed state) without the application being notified about it. This ensures user messaging is correct and reflects the specific failure properly. Also note the transmitter does not have any mechanism to notify the application of state changes, so this watchdog performs the entire role of this dynamic detection. The watchdog is only applicable in error scenarios, and does not activate under normal usage.

When the application is attempting to start a session there is no measurement watchdog, it only applies once a session is "expected" by the application.

Each time the application connects to the transmitter, including after any Bluetooth disconnection, the application runs a number of commands to identify the transmitter as well as identify the running session on the transmitter. The application watchdog is activated after this "startup procedure" is completed, and the application is in one of the "transmitter validated and data ready to receive" states. The watchdog is implemented as a 3 minute in-memory timer which resets when the next expected data packet is received, but if no expected packet arrives it triggers and moves the state machine back to run the "startup procedure" commands again. The "startup procedure" will then perform the appropriate transmitter state check commands and associated procedures for terminal states.

A single watchdog is only ever active, depending on the type of "data ready to receive state":
* If the application is only expecting real-time measurement packets (not RACP packets, no requested RACP range), the watchdog is active to ensure measurement packets arrive successfully.
* If the application is expecting RACP packets the watchdog is active to ensure RACP packets arrive successfully - a lack of measurement packets need not trigger the watchdog until RACP is complete as the no-data alarm will highlight this potential error condition, the watchdog only determines if the transmitter state recheck is required, and as long as it is delivering data this procedure s not ready to be rechecked / interrupted.

Report and bar-chart views follow the same controlled-axis approach by fixing label count, applying discrete tick spacing, and formatting labels so panning, range switching, fullscreen viewing, or chart refresh does not produce overlapping, truncated, or unclear axis labels.

The user confirms a finished or otherwise ended session explicitly through the dashboard UI, with a button press alongside the terminal messaging (session finish can occur for a number of reasons) which always asks them to confirm they understand the sensor is no longer generating measurements, and they are also told that the button will stop collection of data and alarms for their CGM. Only after this button is pressed are they shown the guidance to replace their sensor. If the CGM is still fetching measurements from RACP during the terminal state (i.e. completed sensor), the UI to end the session is not displayed until this is complete (and in this scenario the application has no choice but to sound the no-data alarm (the user can snooze the no-data alarm) until it is fully complete). Note that old measurements are not expected to be fetching for any substantial period of time while the CGM is in the completed state.

In the unlikely case the application is still fetching historical measurements via RACP after the sensor terminates, it will continue doing so, and the user won't have the option to confirm session end (the button will be / appear disabled) until this is complete - Messaging will inform the user their session has ended but that they need to wait for measurements to sync from the transmitter before installing a new sensor. In this scenario the no-data alarm will continue to function to alert the user to the lack of real-time data and alarming, and the user will have to snooze it (repeatedly if necessary) until the historical data fetch is complete.

A finished or otherwise ended session is tracked by the presence of a number of terminal CGM states, retained in memory. If the application is terminated, it will reconnect to the CGM and determine the same state-based terminal state. The application disconnects once it sees this state (to allow the user to connect with a different mobile phone subsequently), but retains the terminal state in memory.
Sheet1 ROW 302 | 1: DI-867 | 2: DO-839 | 3: The application does not have authentication failure conditions which cause the logout procedures to be executed. The only way these procedures are executed is after explicit user action on the "logout" menu option, followed by acceptance of the disclaimer that logout will end their session.

The application handles OAuth authentication failures which require token refresh transparently, and more permanent authentication errors share handling with the generic case for other non-200 error codes (not network errors).

User messaging is handled by DO-722 the same "unable to backup / check for safe usage" notification that appears if the server has been uncontactable for a long period of time.
Sheet1 ROW 303 | 1: DI-870 | 2: DO-927 | 3: Low and medium priority notifications cannot interfere with each other by design - Multiple are tracked and permitted simultaneously, and the user can receive multiple of these simultaneously, with periodic repeats of each medium priority notification tracked on a shared timer for simplicity (this does mean that in the case of multiple medium priority events some of the medium priority notifications will initially repeat more regularly than the 15 minutes specified, to initially align with the already running shared timer).

Critical priority alarms are designed so that multiple critical priority alarms at the same time have the following priority order:
* Critical low glucose alarm - this is always the highest priority critical alarm and will show above all others.
* Critical no-data alarm - this can overlap with the actual critical low glucose alarm if the critical low glucose alarm is continuing to show / sound due to no user interaction, and the no-data alarm then activates. It ensures no continuity gap with the critical low glucose alarm, and to ensure this both can be active at the same time and will need to be snoozed one after the other. If the no-data alarm is triggering at critical level due to a "last available measurement" that is past the critically low glucose threshold, the no-data alarm triggers itself, as well as a critical low glucose alarm if the low glucose alarm is not already sounding.
* Critical recall alarm - sounds at a lower priority than the other critical alarms.
* Critical no-data direct boot alarm - can never display at the same time as other alarms (and this is ensured by the primary application so that even if the system calls the direct boot hook while the main application is loaded and active, the direct boot alarm will never trigger), the direct boot alarm does not utilise the application database as it is not available at that time due to encryption.

Cyber ROW 16 | 1: CVSS / CVE | 2: Exploitability metrics and the Impact metrics. | 7: The Exploitability metrics reflect the ease and technical means by which the vulnerability can be exploited. That is, they represent characteristics of the “thing that is vulnerable”, which we refer to formally as the “vulnerable system”. The Impact metrics reflect the direct consequence of a successful exploit, and represent the consequence to the “things that suffer the impact”, which may include impact on the vulnerable system and/or the downstream impact on what is formally called the “subsequent system(s)”.
Cyber ROW 17 | 2: CVSS is composed of four metric groups: Base (“Attack Complexity” (AC) and “Attack Requirements” (AT)), Threat, Environmental, and Supplemental, each consisting of a set of metrics, as shown in Figure 1.
Cyber ROW 18 | 7: The Base metric group represents the intrinsic characteristics of a vulnerability that are constant over time and across user environments. It is composed of two sets of metrics: the Exploitability metrics and the Impact metrics. | 8: When the Base metrics are assigned values by an analyst, the Base metrics assessment results in a score ranging from 0.0 to 10.0.
Cyber ROW 19 | 7: The Threat metric group reflects the characteristics of a vulnerability related to threat that may change over time but not necessarily across user environments. For example, confirmation that the vulnerability has neither been exploited nor has any proof-of-concept exploit code or instructions publicly available will lower the resulting CVSS score. The values found in this metric group may change over time. | 8: Generally, the Base metrics are specified by vulnerability bulletin analysts, product vendors, or application vendors because they typically possess the most accurate information about the characteristics of a vulnerability. The Threat and Environmental metrics are specified by consumer organizations because they are best able to assess the potential impact of a vulnerability within their own computing environment, at a given point in time.
Cyber ROW 20 | 7: The Environmental metric group represents the characteristics of a vulnerability that are relevant and unique to a particular consumers’ environment. Considerations include the presence of security controls which may mitigate some or all consequences of a successful attack, and the relative importance of a vulnerable system within a technology infrastructure.
Cyber ROW 21 | 7: The Supplemental metric group includes metrics that provide context as well as describe and measure additional extrinsic attributes of a vulnerability. The response to each metric within the Supplemental metric group is to be determined by the CVSS consumer, allowing the usage of an end-user risk analysis system to apply locally significant severity to the metrics and values. No metric will, within its specification, have any impact on the final CVSS score (e.g. CVSS-BTE). Consumer organizations may then assign importance and/or effective impact of each metric, or set/combination of metrics, giving them more, less, or absolutely no effect on the categorization, prioritization, and assessment of the vulnerability. Metrics and values will simply convey additional extrinsic characteristics of the vulnerability itself.
